techniques.name: Patch pipeline (patches -> city -> wards -> blocks -> lots)
techniques.algorithm_summary: Map partitioned into cells ('patches'); central few marked 'city'; most city patches are 'regular'; regular patches cut into blocks; the cuts become streets. Creator says unchanged in essence since the 2017 first version. Size param = patch count; Medium = 20-40 patches (was 12-25), ~1000-2000 buildings, ~6.3 people/building.
techniques.biggest_unknown: How patches themselves are generated, and the ward-type assignment rules beyond 'regular'.

techniques.name: District-wide street construction (patch merging, 0.10.0)
techniques.algorithm_summary: Merge adjacent same-district patches into one polygon, then run twisted bisection on the merged polygon so cuts cross former cell edges. Makes cells invisible and creates an illusion of streets following terrain - explicitly 'just twisted bisection propagating properties of the outer shape inside'. Caused the alpha's instability because merged polygons are strongly concave.
techniques.biggest_unknown: The district partition itself (which patches merge) and how merged concave boundaries are conditioned before cutting.

techniques.name: Twisted bisection (block + lot subdivision primitive)
techniques.algorithm_summary: Recursive bisection with curved rather than straight cut lines, inherited from Neighbourhood Generator; replaced plain recursive bisection of patches in 0.9.0. Propagates outer-boundary shape inward. Breaks on complex concave shapes via collapsed/intersecting edges. A user stack trace shows a per-polygon 'rect' (oriented bounding box) going null on degenerate input.
techniques.biggest_unknown: The actual twist construction - cut control points, curvature derivation, recursion stop conditions, degeneracy guards. Detailed only in post 49191011, outside this slice.

techniques.name: Lots methods: Bisection / Voronoi / Twisted
techniques.algorithm_summary: Three interchangeable block-to-footprint partitioners exposed as a dropdown in 0.9.0. Bisection is the original and judged inferior; Voronoi pairs with 'Simple' display; Twisted pairs with 'Lots' display and the generator auto-switches to highlight the pairing. Whole dropdown deleted in 0.11.1 as over-optioned.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Which one survived as the sole method after 0.11.1, and the Voronoi seeding rule inside a block.

techniques.name: Lot post-processing: Shrink / Offset
techniques.algorithm_summary: Shrink = inward polygon offset per lot leaving gaps (removed 0.11.1). Offset = shift the street-facing ('front') side of every lot so facade lines become uneven; works best with twisted lots. Implies each lot carries a known street-frontage edge.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Magnitude/distribution of the front-side shift and how the front edge is identified.

techniques.name: Perimeter blocks with courtyards
techniques.algorithm_summary: Every block renders as a ring of lots around an empty interior void; courtyard width scales with block size and small blocks have none. Creator confirms trees are placed in 'empty spaces inside blocks (shared courtyards)'. Consistent with subdividing only an inward-offset boundary band of each block.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Whether the band depth is a constant, a fraction of block size, or an emergent result of the lot algorithm.

techniques.name: Outskirts filtering
techniques.algorithm_summary: To de-urbanise the fringe, street density is decreased outward while building density along the surviving streets stays high. Produces ribbon development along radial roads with empty wedges between. Named a 'filter', so streets are generated then discarded.
techniques.biggest_unknown: What the falloff is a function of (radius, ring index, per-patch attribute) and the discard criterion.

techniques.name: Geometry smoothing (coast, walls, roads, district borders)
techniques.algorithm_summary: 0.10.0 added much better smoothing of coast/walls/roads (roads had looked jagged inside city limits); 0.10.1 improved curved-alley and district-border shapes, stated to both look more organic and reduce twisted-bisection glitches. Walls go from visibly polygonal (0.9.0) to smooth polylines with large turning radii.
techniques.biggest_unknown: The smoothing method - Chaikin, spline resample or offset-and-resample - is never named.

techniques.name: Two road classes: main roads vs alleys
techniques.algorithm_summary: Main roads radiate centre-to-map-edge and have 'a completely different nature' from alleys; alleys are the block cut lines and come in two sub-types that are never explained. Main roads pass through wall gates and continue off-map; road bearings align with a parent region map only for coastal towns, because those are oriented relative to the coast.
techniques.biggest_unknown: How main roads are constructed at all - no method is given anywhere in this slice.

techniques.name: Explicit alley rendering (0.10.2)
techniques.algorithm_summary: Rendering-only change: the alley graph already existed as block cut lines and is now drawn as ribbons (key A), exported to JSON, and combinable with Display mode Hidden (key B) for a pure street map. Alleys deliberately do not look identical to major roads.
techniques.biggest_unknown: The 'nuances' that made alleys render differently from major roads.

techniques.name: Straight-skeleton roof details (Plain/Hip/Gable, 0.11.0)
techniques.algorithm_summary: Roof detail derived from the footprint's straight skeleton: hip roofs show a ridge plus hip lines to corners; long footprints become a row of gable bays. Drawn as line work only, not filled faces. Interacts with Raised (view from slightly lower); raised gables look like greenhouses - a known unfixed flaw.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Gable construction (ridge-direction choice and end-wall handling) and the hip/gable selection rule per building.

techniques.name: Curved labels along a straight-skeleton ridge (0.11.1)
techniques.algorithm_summary: Replaced the creator's own heuristic (labels escaped their polygons and sometimes bent the wrong way) with a 'widely used' algorithm: draw the area label along a ridge of the area's straight skeleton. Which ridge is suitable is admittedly ambiguous. Shipped with letter-spacing and text-outline fixes. Label size scales with district area.

techniques.name: District View (0.11.0)
techniques.algorithm_summary: Substitute for real zoom (declared 'too difficult for a specific technical reason') and for NG integration. Shift-click a district; it fills the viewport, everything else hidden, drawn at exactly the same detail as city view. District border drawn as a thick semi-transparent dashed line over water and walls. PNG/SVG export the district; JSON still exports the whole city.
techniques.biggest_unknown: The technical reason real zoom is impossible - likely scale-baked line widths/text/detail thresholds, but unverified.

techniques.name: Tree placement (three generations)
techniques.algorithm_summary: 0.9.1: trees in city greens, block courtyards, occasionally between farm fields; no density control by design. 0.9.2: fluffier and smaller, a different much faster placement method whose side effect is visibly more trees. 0.10.2: smaller and more irregular, drawn with the NG tree algorithm at reduced detail. Rendered as clustered lobed blobs, including hedgerow chains along field edges.
techniques.biggest_unknown: None of the three placement algorithms is named; only relative speed and density side-effects are recorded.

techniques.name: Forests (0.11.4)
techniques.algorithm_summary: Forest = complement of (city + farmland + water) over the map, filled as one flat mass with a scalloped edge of overlapping circular lobes. Roads are drawn over the forest rather than clearing it - an explicit draw-order choice. Known flaw: edges look too straight on large maps. Broke PNG export; the speculative fix lowers export resolution when forests are on.
techniques.biggest_unknown: The standoff/offset distance defining the cleared area and the lobe parameterisation; and why large maps produce straight edges.

techniques.name: Farm fields
techniques.algorithm_summary: Irregular quad patchwork tiling the ring between the built-up edge and the forest/map edge, separated by narrow ground-coloured lanes, with isolated farm buildings. Per-field furrow hatching with independent direction, or a solid fill option (0.10.2). 0.9.1 changed spawning to hide 'sawtooths' of the farmland border; 0.10.2 made fields always generated and only style-hidden.
techniques.biggest_unknown: The tessellation method and what the 0.9.1 sawtooth fix actually changed.

techniques.name: Water system: coasts, bays, rivers, piers, water gates
techniques.algorithm_summary: Declared dated and primitive in 0.9.0 with a stated goal of arbitrary land/water configurations (islands, river confluences, wide rivers) - still unshipped by 2025. 0.11.2 changed bay generation to be more diverse and removed 'headlands' (inverted bays) as ugly. techniques.biggest_unknown: Any method at all for coast/river/bay shape; only outcomes and a roadmap are recorded.

techniques.name: Walls, towers, gates and the castle/citadel enclosure
techniques.algorithm_summary: Closed smooth wall polyline with towers at vertices (round; 'Open' half-towers added 0.9.0; Bastions removed 0.11.0) and wider blocks at gates where main roads cross; wall terminates at water leaving a water gate. URL exposes walls, citadel, urban_castle, gates as switches.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Placement and shape rules for the castle enclosure and gate count/position selection.

techniques.name: Tints and weathering colour model
techniques.algorithm_summary: District tints derived from a base colour by one of three methods - Spectrum, Brightness, Overlay - with a Strength percentage (default 50). All outlines share one 'Dark' colour; per-class outline toggles added 0.9.1.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Exact colour maths for each method and the weathering distribution.

techniques.algorithm_summary: Unreleased: non-uniform building heights requiring z-sorting (painter's algorithm); oblique/military projection with per-face flat shading; roof faces as filled polygons with back-face culling instead of wireframe lines; single directional light with uniform-length ground shadows; roof hatching for texture. techniques.algorithm_summary: SVG rewritten in 0.9.0 from a 'universal' method first built for Perilous Shores; only hatching unsupported (text and gradients were the PS-era gaps). JSON is one-way, for third parties and City Viewer only; grew to carry district descriptions, trees and alleys. Permalinks encode generator parameters only - district renames and landmarks are lost, and round-trips can subtly change geometry.

techniques.algorithm_summary: Armoria supplies coats of arms (random in 0.8.2, specific design + legend embedding in 0.8.3; import-by-link and emblem tinting announced but unshipped). top_insights: The whole-pipeline statement in post 87882877 is the single most valuable text in this slice: patches -> a few central patches marked 'city' -> most become 'regular' -> regular patches cut into blocks -> the cuts are the streets; unchanged in essence since 2017.

The 0.10.0 breakthrough is merging patches so streets are cut district-wide, which hides the cell structure and fakes an underlying landscape - and this concave-polygon input is exactly what destabilised twisted bisection for six months.

Twisted bisection is the load-bearing primitive used twice (alleys and lots); it is the largest reproduction gap here, and a user stack trace reveals a per-polygon oriented-rectangle step that goes null on degenerate geometry.
Straight skeletons do double duty: roof detail in 0.11.0 and label-along-the-ridge placement in 0.11.1 - one geometry kernel powering two visually unrelated features.
Blocks are perimeter rings with courtyard voids, and those voids are what the trees feature fills; the lot generator almost certainly subdivides only an inward-offset boundary band.

Forests are a pure complement operation - everything not city, farmland or water - drawn under roads with a scalloped lobed edge; the creator's own complaint about straight edges on large maps points at a fixed offset distance.
Main roads are stated to be of 'a completely different nature' from alleys, yet no method for them is described anywhere in this slice - a genuine blank in the reconstruction.
Design philosophy is explicit and consistent: readability over fancy 3D, option count as a liability (four options deleted in 0.11.1), and deliberate visual convergence with Neighbourhood Generator.
Hard numbers recovered: Medium = 20-40 patches (was 12-25), 1000-2000 buildings, ~6.3 people per building (2702 buildings / ~17000 pop), Procgen Mansion cell ~3 m, tint Strength 50%.
A full URL parameter surface is captured verbatim from a comment: size, seed, name, population, greens, farms, citadel, urban_castle, plaza, temple, walls, shantytown, coast, river, gates, sea.

top_insights: Two 0.11.x releases hand over the same primitive: straight skeleton drives BOTH hip/gable roof geometry (0.11.0) and curvilinear district labels (0.11.1). One skeleton implementation likely serves both - the highest-leverage thing to build first.

The 0.9.0 Style>Buildings panel leaks the entire lot pipeline as four named stages (Lots method / Filter lots / Processing / Display mode) with values 'Twisted', 'Offset', 'Lots' - the closest thing to a spec for MFCG's building generation anywhere in this slice.
Population is exactly 6.29 x building count (286->~1800, 2702->~17000, agreeing to 4 significant figures). Deterministic and linear, not a per-building random draw.

Watabou states the generator's metric scale is wrong - 'buildings often seem way too large' - so footprint size, road width, scale bar and population are all mutually mis-calibrated. A re-implementation must choose to reproduce or fix this deliberately.

OpenFL made real zoom impossible for the whole 6-year span, which forced two design consequences: framing had to be solved at generation time, and 'zoom' shipped as shift+click district re-render. A fixed-resolution render target is the single most consequential architectural constraint visible here.
Negative space is authored before subdivision, not repaired after: small plazas are stamped around gates as keep-out polygons so buildings never overlap gates (0.7.3 fix).

GeoJSON export metadata is degree-scaled and decodable: roadWidth ~8m, towerRadius == wallThickness ~7.6m, riverWidth ~34m at lat 40. Towers are exactly as thick as the wall - a modelling fact, not rounding.

Voronoi is confirmed as the foundation by the author's own retrospective ('barely more than stylized Voronoi diagrams'), and the Delaunator swap made it 100x faster while explicitly NOT being the bottleneck - the cost is downstream in lots and rendering.
The post.md 'date' fields are a scrape artifact (22 of 23 read 03 Feb 2025). Version numbers and Patreon post ids are the only reliable chronology for this slice.

techniques.name: Population-density map (shared driver field)
techniques.algorithm_summary: A 2-D scalar field named by watabou as the 'population density map'. Drives (a) village-square siting at its peak, (b) house packing tightness, (c) built-up extent, (d) palisade shape AND radius. Biased toward the highway ('often it's a place on the highway'). Sparse vs dense is a per-village amplitude: dense villages pack houses tighter AND get a larger palisade radius on average. Consumed both pointwise (square siting) and as a 2-D iso-contour (palisade shape). Water is a downstream veto, not baked in.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Field construction: kernel shape, highway coupling strength, noise spectrum, resolution, and whether it is recomputed after water is carved.

techniques.name: Village square construction
techniques.algorithm_summary: Full quoted algorithm (devlog 507254): find a high-population-density location, often on the highway; create a circle of 'a reasonable size' there; distort it a little; that becomes the square polygon; if it does not overlap water, add a centrepiece (a large tree or a well). Images confirm both centrepiece branches, distortion amounts from ~0 (perfect circle, Abehorn) to strong (irregular blob, St Roesia), and that the square does NOT scale with population (identical at pop. 180 and pop. 1700). A third centrepiece case (a building on the square) appears in the default-style image, unexplained.
techniques.biggest_unknown: The 'reasonable size' formula and the exact distortion operator; full centrepiece table; how roads attach to the square rim.

techniques.name: Palisade from density iso-contour
techniques.algorithm_summary: Enclosure shape derived from the population density map; sparse villages get smaller fences, dense ones larger radius on average. Observed geometry is always a single smooth closed convex-ish curve (egg/ellipse/oval), never terrain-following and never self-intersecting — consistent with a smoothed iso-contour of one dominant density bump. Gates are placed where roads cross the wall (3-4 per map, count = number of crossings). Fields and occasional outlying houses sit outside. Rendered as a dark bank band carrying a line of pale post beads; exported as a polyline plus gate positions (confirmed by the City Viewer 3-D render).
techniques.biggest_unknown: The iso-value/threshold, the smoothing operator, and the size distribution behind '(on average)'.

techniques.name: Recursive bisection with a twist ('bent cuts')
techniques.algorithm_summary: NG's core. Modification of simple recursive bisection where the dividing cut is BENT (a polyline with an interior kink) instead of a straight chord. Creator's two stated reasons: (a) it produces more natural-looking junctions, (b) the recursive nature becomes less visible to the naked eye. Originally intended for MFCG but rejected there as 'too slow and too unstable'; NG 1.0 is a from-scratch reimplementation with 'a better implementation of the bisection idea'. Images show block boundaries kinking mid-segment so house rows turn a few degrees mid-run; streets are the inset gap between cells, not stroked cut lines.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Bend location/angle distribution, cut-direction choice, stopping criterion, and what the stabilisation fix was.

techniques.name: Perimeter-block building placement
techniques.algorithm_summary: Each block is ringed edge-to-edge by narrow rectangles fronting the street, leaving a bare interior courtyard. Reconstructed as: inset the block polygon by building depth, then subdivide the resulting boundary ring into randomly-sized frontages. Roof tones alternate light/dark so individual houses stay legible. Some blocks are left partially built, some are wholly green (grove/garden blocks). The whole block plus courtyard casts one drop shadow, reading as a raised plateau. Categorically different from VG's free-standing road-oriented houses.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Frontage width distribution, depth law, corner handling, and the rule choosing partial/green/built blocks.

techniques.name: Ring template with degenerate-case fallback
techniques.algorithm_summary: One named member of a template system. Lays down one or more concentric ring roads, crossed by radials, then cuts the annuli into wedge blocks with the same bisection machinery. Stated fallback: if the smallest ring is too small to be cut into blocks, a square, a grove, or a single large building is placed there instead. The 'Stone Circle' image visibly exercises the third branch (a hipped-roof mansion on the central plaza). Outer ring is clipped by an independently generated patch outline.
techniques.biggest_unknown: The rest of the template list (1.1.0 says 'templates' plural before ring existed) and the ring-count/radius law.

techniques.name: Recursive field subdivision with lanes and per-parcel furrows
techniques.algorithm_summary: Introduced 1.2.5, rebuilt 1.2.7, improved again 1.5.1. A contiguous farmland region is recursively split by straight cuts into parcels; every cut leaves a gap rendered as a green lane, implying per-parcel inward offsetting rather than drawn lines. Furrow hatch angle is constant within a parcel, differs between parcels, and correlates among siblings — consistent with deriving the angle from each parcel's OBB long axis. Trees are planted along lanes and at corners as hedgerows. 1.5.1 adds a second regime: radial wedge parcels fanning out from the settlement. A third class exists: small crofts/kitchen gardens inside the palisade.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Whether the radial-wedge form is a separate template or polar-space recursion; the area threshold; how many field classes exist and how they are assigned.

techniques.name: House placement and orientation
techniques.algorithm_summary: Never explained in any VG devlog. Observed: rectangles with 2:1-4:1 long axis, in short parallel runs of 2-6 sharing alignment, set back from the road, long axis parallel to the nearest road and tangential around the square (producing fan patterns). Not snapped to a lot grid and not perimeter-ringed. Density tracks the density field, thinning to isolated farmsteads at the edge. Composite L/T footprints exist. A 'wilderness mode' toggle removes all buildings, so they are a detachable layer over a self-sufficient terrain+road+field substrate.
techniques.biggest_unknown: The placement algorithm itself — Poisson-disc with density-varying radius, rejection sampling, and road-frontage plot subdivision all fit the images equally well.

techniques.name: River subsystem (rewritten from scratch in 1.5.2)
techniques.algorithm_summary: Creator states the first river implementation 'looked more or less acceptable, but inside it was a total mess' and that he rewrote everything river-related from scratch rather than refactoring. Behaviour shown: smooth spline-like meanders with varying width, working Y-confluences with the merged channel wider than either tributary, downstream widening into estuary/lake, nested tone bands from bank to centre (implying centreline + width profile rendered by repeated inward offsetting), and a pale sand bank strip from an outward offset.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Whether rivers are traced downhill on the heightfield or drawn top-down with terrain conformed to them; the width law and confluence construction.

techniques.name: Spotlight (adaptive radial vignette)
techniques.algorithm_summary: A post-process soft radial gradient brightening the map's focus and darkening its periphery. Creator: 'similar to vignetting, but it's more customizable and sort of smarter'. Has its own settings window plus a toggle. The 'smarter' part is unexplained; images show the bright pool centred on the settlement rather than the image centre and its radius hugging the built-up extent, so it is most likely auto-fitted to the density peak. Dominant compositional device in dark styles, near-invisible in light ones.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Confirmation of what 'smarter' means — auto-centring on the settlement focus versus some content-aware falloff.

techniques.name: Slope shading vs hachures vs contours (three relief layers)
techniques.algorithm_summary: 1.6.2: ground drawn shaded, sun-facing slopes highlighted and opposite ones darkened; creator notes it 'functionally duplicates hachures'. Keyboard shortcuts prove relief (E) and shading (H) are separate independent toggles, so VG carries a heightfield and exposes it three redundant ways: downslope hachure ticks, contour lines (becoming offshore bathymetric bands over water), and diffuse slope shading applied as full-map luminance modulation beneath everything.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Heightfield source (noise vs erosion), sun azimuth (fixed vs style-controlled), contour interval.

techniques.name: Selective outlining
techniques.algorithm_summary: 1.6.8: object contours rendered using shades of the objects themselves rather than solid black or any fixed colour. Creator names the technique 'selective outlining' and notes it comes from pixel art. Effect: outlines stop fighting the palette in pastel styles, dark styles stop collapsing into black mush, and every style gets coherent line treatment without per-style outline tuning. Highest quality-per-line-of-code item in the slice; watabou retrofitted it after roughly four years of releases.
techniques.biggest_unknown: The exact shade-derivation function (fixed luminance delta, HSL shift, or per-category).

techniques.name: Style as downloadable JSON data
techniques.algorithm_summary: Twelve named style files (vivid, duskvol, haunted, fall, beach, subtle, default, sand, cold, night, bw, minimal) served as JSON, plus six preset slots, a random-style button and a style dialog. The devlog renders all twelve over ONE seed, isolating exactly what style owns. Critically, 'subtle' and 'bw' drop area fills entirely (line-work only) while 'minimal' drops outlines entirely — so the renderer must assume neither fill nor stroke exists. Style controls tree canopy silhouette and a multi-colour tree set (five colours in one confirmed example), roof type including 'Ruin', water banding, and hatch presence.
techniques.biggest_unknown: The style schema itself — which properties are exposed and at what granularity.

techniques.name: JSON export, City Viewer and GET-parameter integration
techniques.algorithm_summary: Cross-generator integration is done entirely through URL GET parameters ('all the integration users requested could be implemented via GET method requests'), keeping apps small and separately deployable; right-clicking a building opens it in Procgen Mansion. Permalinks are seed plus comma-separated tags (?seed=975637253&tags=pond,grove,organic,isolated; crossroads added in 1.6.4). The City Viewer 3-D render reveals the exported model: palisade polyline with gates, building footprints with orientation and height, tree positions with per-instance radii, square polygon with well object, road ribbons with width, field polygons.
techniques.biggest_unknown: The JSON schema in detail, and whether elevation is exported at all (the 3-D viewer renders a flat plane).

techniques.name: Entity-must-reach-every-sink failure mode
techniques.algorithm_summary: 1.6.1: palisades shipped in 1.6.0 without being written to JSON export or rendered in City Viewer — 'I was expecting bug reports related to palisades, but instead I found a whole chunk of functionality missing'. Canonical instance of a write surviving one lifecycle path and ghosting another. Any new map entity must be threaded through generation, 2-D render, JSON export and external viewer; a registration manifest should make it impossible to add one without all four.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Nothing material — this is a process lesson rather than an algorithm.

techniques.name: Shared engine with periodic code transplant between generators
techniques.algorithm_summary: NG 1.2.1: 'I just remembered that I should transplant some of the code from the latest versions of MFCG (and my other generators)'. Explains why NG, VG and MFCG converge on identical style vocabularies, identical landmark categories (VG's square centrepiece 'a large tree or a well' vs NG's pins 'fountains, wells and large trees'), identical export plumbing and identical shortcut grammar. Implies the right architecture is one shared engine (geometry, style, render, export) with thin per-product layout templates.
techniques.biggest_unknown: How much is actually shared versus copy-pasted, and which subsystems are the common ones.

top_insights: The itch.io VG/NG devlogs are teasers, not documentation - 15 of 21 VG posts are under 110 words and break off at a Patreon link. Only four passages in the whole slice contain real algorithm prose: village square (507254), palisade/density coupling (736720), river rewrite (589997), bent cuts (315495). The images are the primary evidence and carry most of the extraction.

VG's spine is one shared scalar field, the 'population density map', which simultaneously fixes the square's site, house packing, built-up extent and the palisade's shape and radius. Counter-intuitively and explicitly: DENSE villages get a LARGER palisade radius, not a tighter one.

Village square algorithm is stated verbatim and is fully reproducible in outline: density peak (often on the highway) -> circle of reasonable size -> distort a little -> water-overlap test -> centrepiece (large tree or well). Images show distortion ranging from zero to strong, and the square never scales with population (same size at pop. 180 and pop. 1700).

NG's 'bent cuts' are justified aesthetically, not geometrically: the stated purpose is that the recursion must be UNREADABLE to the eye, plus more natural junctions. The technique was rejected from MFCG for being 'too slow and too unstable' - a direct robustness warning - and NG exists as the stabilisation testbed.

NG's ring template supplies a directly reusable degenerate-case pattern, stated by the creator: when a subdivision target is too small to cut into blocks, substitute a landmark (a square, a grove, or a single large building) rather than tolerate slivers.

VG and NG use categorically different block regimes from the same shared engine: VG places free-standing houses in open plots oriented to the nearest road (fanning tangentially around the square), NG rings each block's perimeter edge-to-edge leaving a courtyard. This is the main lever between 'village' and 'town quarter' feel.

The 12-style collection renders one identical seed twelve ways and proves the renderer must survive extremes: 'subtle' and 'bw' drop area fills entirely (line-work only) while 'minimal' drops outlines entirely. Neither fill nor stroke may be assumed to exist, and the geometry layer must therefore expose semantic categories rather than drawing instructions.

Selective outlining (1.6.8) - outline colour derived as a shade of each object's own fill rather than a fixed black - is the highest quality-per-effort rendering idea in the slice, and watabou only retrofitted it after roughly four years. Adopt it from day one.

The 1.6.1 palisade bug is the canonical 'write survives one path, ghosts another' failure: palisades shipped without JSON export or City Viewer support. Every new entity must be threaded through generation, 2-D render, JSON export and external viewer.

Architectural stance is stated outright: many small apps rather than one mega-app, with cross-generator integration done entirely through URL GET parameters, plus periodic code transplant from MFCG into the smaller generators (NG 1.2.1). Mirror it as one shared engine plus thin per-product layout templates.
Map scale is stated in a comment: roughly 200-300 metres across for a 300x300 map - a village and its immediate fields, not a parish. Rendered populations span 96 to 1700 on the same machinery.

Only 2 of 21 VG devlogs add settlement structure (square+orchards, palisades). Everything else is terrain, water, rendering or plumbing - VG's layout core was effectively frozen from 1.2.x and the product improved almost entirely through terrain and render quality.

Two subsystems the creator flags as harder than they look: rivers ('inside it was a total mess', rewritten from scratch rather than refactored) and non-square maps ('took much time to implement and debug it. Too much time'). Build aspect-ratio independence and a replaceable water subsystem in from the start.

The keyboard-shortcut lists are the best architecture readout available: VG's 12 independent layer toggles (relief, fields, shading, orchards, shadows, buildings/wilderness, roads, outlines, nameplate, grid, trees, spotlight) and NG's 6, plus a trees-only reroll in VG, prove per-layer sub-seeds rather than one global RNG stream.
open_questions: How are VG houses actually placed? No devlog explains it. Poisson-disc with density-varying radius, rejection sampling against the density field, and road-frontage plot subdivision all fit the images equally well. Biggest single gap in the VG slice.
How is VG's street network generated? Radial spokes plus concentric arcs around the square are obvious in the images, but the construction (grown, subdivided, or offset rings) is unrecovered.
Construction of the population-density map: kernel shape, highway coupling strength, noise spectrum, grid resolution, and whether it is recomputed after rivers are carved.
NG bent-cut parameters: where along the cut the bend sits, the bend-angle distribution, one kink or several, angular or smoothed, and how cut direction is chosen.
What made bent-cut bisection 'too slow and too unstable' for MFCG, and what the 'better implementation' fixed. This is exactly the robustness knowledge most needed and it is entirely absent.
The palisade iso-value/threshold and smoothing operator, plus the size distribution behind 'larger radius (on average)'.

Is VG's radial-wedge field system a separate template or the same recursive cutter applied in polar coordinates? How many field classes exist (crop, pasture, fallow, orchard, croft) and how are they assigned?
River generation direction: traced downhill on a heightfield, or drawn top-down with terrain conformed to them? Plus the width law and how confluence geometry is built.
What changed in VG 1.6.3 and 1.6.6 - both are absent from the itch devlog stream entirely.
What 'numbered houses' (1.6.4) actually renders: no numbers are legible at published resolution. Small pale tabs on the street-facing side of houses may be number plaques or entrances; unconfirmed.
What 'improved roads' meant in each of VG 1.2.7 and 1.5.4 - two separate unexplained passes.
The full NG template list: 1.1.0 announces 'templates' plural before 'ring' was added in 1.2.0, so at least two more templates existed and are unnamed.
How NG's ragged organic patch outline (which clips every template) is generated - never discussed in any NG post.
Whether elevation is exported to JSON at all: the City Viewer 3-D render shows a flat ground plane despite VG carrying a heightfield.

Confirmation of what makes Spotlight 'sort of smarter' than vignetting - most likely auto-centring on the settlement focus with radius fitted to the built-up extent, but this is inference from images.
The style JSON schema: which properties are exposed and at what granularity (the 12 style files are referenced by URL but their contents are not in this slice).
VG orchard selection rule: what fraction of parcels become orchards, proximity requirements, row spacing, and whether walled orchards were ever implemented (requested in comments, never answered).

techniques.name: Intersection-indexed road graph (persistence model)
techniques.algorithm_summary: Roads stored as (startIntersectionId, endIntersectionId) over an intersection table {id, coordinate}, replacing (startCoord,endCoord). Connectivity = shared integer id, avoiding float-equality failures. Prerequisite for face traversal and safe editing. Shipped pre-release so all towns could be wiped instead of migrated.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Whether a road carries interior vertices (images show multi-bend polylines) or every bend is a degree-2 intersection; whether generator emits the same structure.

techniques.name: Fill tool: raycast seed + left-hand-rule face traversal
techniques.algorithm_summary: Click -> raycast to find first bounding road -> walk the road graph always taking the leftmost successor at each junction ('classic maze trick') until returning to start -> the visited junction coordinates are the fill polygon. Leftmost chosen by signed angle from incoming direction. Standard planar-face extraction stated informally.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Whether the fill result is stored as a frozen point list or as a reference to the bounding road cycle; exact angle-selection convention.

techniques.name: Road-edit snapping: intersection snap + first-crossing split
techniques.algorithm_summary: New roads snap to nearby existing intersections and truncate at the first crossing with an existing road, materialising an intersection there and splitting the crossed road in two. Invariant: no overlap without an intersection, else the left-hand walk escapes the cell.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Snap radius/tolerance; whether generated roads are subject to the same invariant (bug reports imply not).

techniques.name: Two-phase pipeline: generate settlement, then generate map
techniques.algorithm_summary: Step 1 creates the buildings and people (contents). Step 2 takes that building list and assigns every building a location. Inverse of watabou's geometry-first approach. Content order: people/factions -> buildings -> district grouping -> road network -> lot claiming.
techniques.biggest_unknown: How the layout stage guarantees capacity for every pre-committed building.

techniques.name: OLD building selection: resource-demand model
techniques.algorithm_summary: Residents create demands; each placed building satisfies some demand and creates others; greedily place the building satisfying the largest current demand until target population. Shops placed when a demand's import amount crosses one global hard-coded threshold. Worked example given with exact numbers (tailor 100/200, weaver 100/100, farm 50).
techniques.biggest_unknown: The real default demand tables; how population target maps to loop termination.

techniques.name: NEW building selection: building groups + dependency graph
techniques.algorithm_summary: Buildings belong to groups. Each group has a rule: 1 per N people, or 1 per N buildings of other group(s). Within-group weighted proportions; lifestyle-conditioned candidate rows; shop alternatives with optional custom shop percentage; 'ignore rules for first building' + population threshold guarantees one instance. ~8% faster than the demand model.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Evaluation order (topological vs fixed-point), cycle handling, reconciliation with the population target.

techniques.name: OLD district formation: lifestyle grouping + lot claiming
techniques.algorithm_summary: Group buildings by lifestyle -> generate road network (lots = faces) -> a district claims a lot and fills it -> overflow claims an adjacent lot -> if none, start a new district of that type elsewhere -> repeat until all buildings placed. Failure modes he names: random-feeling contents, no identity, wasted space in oversized lots.
techniques.biggest_unknown: How a lot is chosen to claim, what 'adjacent' means, and how buildings are arranged inside a lot.

techniques.name: NEW district formation: overall districts + sub-districts + empty-space backfill
techniques.algorithm_summary: Overall district (lifestyle or major industry) owns multiple sub-districts (e.g. clothing, metalwork); every building has a preferred sub-district; buildings group on (lifestyle, preferred sub-district); a parent district places its sub-districts in order. Empty space is now backfilled with randomly picked buildings matching the district's (sub-district, lifestyle) - so layout can invent contents.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Sub-district ordering rule and how districts are seeded relative to water/centre/walls.

techniques.name: Lot -> plot -> building hierarchy with edge-frontage vs dense regimes
techniques.algorithm_summary: Reconstructed from before/after images and the district config vocabulary: lots are road-graph faces; default 'buildings only on lot edge' produces a one-deep perimeter ring of abutting burgage-style plots with long axis perpendicular to the street and a residual courtyard; 'dense + not-on-lot-edge' tiles the whole lot polygon with banded quadrilateral plots. Each plot carries a background texture, a building and optional decoration.
techniques.biggest_unknown: The actual subdivision algorithm (recursive longest-axis split vs offsetting vs clipped grid) - never stated anywhere.

techniques.name: Decoration system: background texture / plot / lot-edge / lot decoration, dense vs sparse phases
techniques.algorithm_summary: District config exposes: Building background textures (Grass/Lawn/Dirt/Road), Lot decoration (Park, Park with fountain, Plaza, Plaza with fountain, Plaza with well, Dirt), Lot edge decoration (Trees), weighted Plot decoration (Trees, Grass, Garden fences, Well, Fountain, Bandstand, Statue, Monument, Campfire). Two decoration profiles per district (Dense/Sparse) plus per-phase building modifier and material, and a 'can be placed during dense phase when' rule.
techniques.biggest_unknown: What the dense and sparse phases actually are, their order, and the full enums.

techniques.name: Walls placed at build-progress checkpoints (multiple concentric rings)
techniques.algorithm_summary: Military config has 'When to place walls' = a table of 'Estimate percentage of buildings within wall' rows (20.00, 60.00 shown) with + Add wall. Reading: layout is incremental, and at each listed completion fraction a wall is built around the current built extent - producing historic concentric rings with roughly convex, ~14-20 vertex outlines and round towers at direction changes. Corroborated by a two-ring city image.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Hull/offset method and slack for the wall polygon, tower spacing rule, and whether gates are real objects that snap roads.

techniques.name: Lifestyle-driven district appearance (squalid tents, poor dense, wealthy decorated)
techniques.algorithm_summary: Defaults per lifestyle on the six-level ladder (Squalid, Poor, Modest, Comfortable, Wealthy, Aristocratic): squalid renders as randomly-rotated small square tents with four-facet pyramid shading in saturated random colours on dirt, unaligned to lot edges; poor is maximally dense; wealthy gets large footprints, trees, wells, fountains and paved plazas. Roof materials include red/blue tile and custom colours.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Tent footprint size distribution and the scatter rule that replaces lot-edge alignment.

techniques.name: Manual water drawing: rivers vs oceans, bridge spacing constraint
techniques.algorithm_summary: Water configuration = Generated | Manually drawn. Rivers are bridgeable, oceans are not. Draw canvas shows the generation-area bounds and the settlement centre, with Draw river / Draw ocean / Demolish; water drawn as variable-width stroked polylines and closed blobs. 'Required distance between bridges' = 100. Lakes, branching rivers and islands became possible in both manual and generated modes.
techniques.biggest_unknown: The entire generated-water branch (river paths, coastlines, branching, lakes) and how the bridge-spacing constraint is enforced.

techniques.name: District naming with landmark detection and name erosion
techniques.algorithm_summary: Name parts drawn from sub-district vocabulary plus detected physical landmarks (wall, tower, gate, pass, market, docks). Names erode over time into shorthand: 'Hamlet Tower' -> 'Hamower'. Map labels corroborate (SOUTATE=South Gate, ESTPASS, ESTFORGE, WALLAZAAR, FLEASTEAD), and some names stay uneroded, so erosion is probabilistic.
techniques.biggest_unknown: The elision algorithm itself and what qualifies as a landmark.

techniques.name: Re-roll district
techniques.algorithm_summary: Reuses the empty-space backfill algorithm: deletes existing buildings and decoration in a user-drawn district and regenerates buildings plus new people. Settings: overall lifestyle, generation type (e.g. 'Residential, with basic shops'), default lifestyle decoration, buildings-not-on-lot-edge, dense buildings, building modifier, building material.
techniques.biggest_unknown: How the re-roll region maps onto existing lots and how new people are wired into the existing social graph.

techniques.name: Schedule and sub-location simulation model
techniques.algorithm_summary: Per-day-group schedules (7-day week) of entries: time range + status (Sleeping/Working/...) + primary behaviour criteria (e.g. 'Primary location has other occupants', 'Fifty percent chance') + Primary and Default behaviours. A behaviour = action text + building matcher (Place of work, Exact building, Fetch demanded resources) + sub-location matcher (Exact sub-location, Random with tag). Sub-locations have per-purpose capacity limits and tags (Room, Table, Sell goods, Pickup goods, Deliver goods, Performance, Bath, Custom 1-5). Schedules lazy-loaded by job: file -5%, generation -5%, simulation -20%.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Routing between sub-locations (pathfinding vs teleport), whether travel consumes time, and the full status/matcher enums.

techniques.name: Event generation from relations and factions
techniques.algorithm_summary: Per building, generate 10 candidate events drawn from the person-relation graph (business/competitive/religious/romantic rivals, crushes, separated partners, affairs) and faction goals/methods. 'Start event' executes it: moves the involved people around the settlement and mutates their relations. Event text templates were drafted with ChatGPT; selection and execution are hand-coded.
techniques.biggest_unknown: How the 10 candidates are selected and ranked, and the full set of state mutations 'Start event' performs.

techniques.name: Per-race appearance template system
techniques.algorithm_summary: Per race: weighted random tables labelled per attribute (e.g. Hair length: bald 50, cropped 50, short 50, medium-length 50, long 25, very long 25) plus a multi-line text template referencing $option1..$optionN, $height and $aOrAn. Lines have display conditions on gender, age and the option values. Rendered once at generation and persisted (fixes apply only to new settlements).
techniques.biggest_unknown: The condition expression language on lines.

techniques.name: Genders, pronouns and the attraction weight matrix
techniques.algorithm_summary: Genders are data with weights (male 47, female 47, non-binary 5, agender 1), each carrying subject/object pronoun, possessive adjective, name type and height config. Pairing is driven by a symmetric N x N gender-relations weight matrix (male-female 92, male-male 4, female-female 4, non-binary 3, agender 1).
techniques.biggest_unknown: How the matrix combines with age, religion and proximity when forming couples.

techniques.name: Export and integration surface (GeoJSON, SVG, FoundryVTT)
techniques.algorithm_summary: GeoJSON export and an SVG export overhaul shipped April 2023 with no schema given; a FoundryVTT module exposes full building/person/event/time access, player sync and a party-location marker, with the Foundry origin URL entered into FTG. No public API and no seed/URL reproducibility model - settlements are server-side persistent objects.
techniques.biggest_unknown: The GeoJSON feature/property schema and the layer decomposition it implies.

top_insights: FTG inverts watabou's pipeline: it generates CONTENTS first (buildings + people + factions), then generates the map as a placement problem over that fixed list. Stated verbatim in post 91451446; corroborated by 'factions are generated before buildings are placed' in the 84680671 comments.

Walls are historic snapshots, not a designed ring: the Military config is a table of 'Estimate percentage of buildings within wall' rows (20% and 60% shown, '+ Add wall'), meaning layout is incremental and a wall is built around the current built extent at each completion fraction. This is the cleanest mechanism in the slice for generating plausible concentric medieval walls.

The district settings UI is a direct window onto the internal spatial model: district -> lot -> plot -> building, with decoration hooks at each level (building background texture, plot decoration, lot edge decoration, lot decoration) and two placement phases (dense/sparse) each with its own material and modifier. The beige core / green suburb look is an emergent sum of per-plot background textures, not a painted district polygon.

The only geometric algorithm named in the whole slice is the map-editor fill tool: raycast to find a bounding road, then walk the road graph always taking the leftmost successor until you return to start - i.e. planar face extraction. Its stated failure mode ('sometimes just fills half of the town' on generated streets) proves the generated road graph is not reliably planar-with-intersections.

The intersection-id refactor (roads as (startId,endId) over an intersection table) was done explicitly because float coordinate equality fails; the invariant 'any crossing must split both edges' is stated by the creator as the intended rule and as a known unfixed bug source.

Building selection was rewritten from a resource-demand priority model to a building-group dependency graph ('1 farm per 25 people', '1 weaver per 2 farms', '1 tailor per 2 weavers') purely for config legibility - and got 8% faster. Real weights are recoverable: Tavern group row 2 = Quiet bar 8.0, Raucous dive 5.0, Secret society 0.5, Gambling den/Casino/Brothel 1.0 each.

Everything is lifestyle-keyed on a six-level ladder (Squalid, Poor, Modest, Comfortable, Wealthy, Aristocratic): building candidates, district decoration, density, roof material and even render mode (squalid districts render as randomly-rotated four-facet pyramid tents in saturated colours).

Rendering conventions are consistent and reproducible: fixed top-left light, soft down-right drop shadows, roofs split by a ridge into differently-lit facets, dotted lot/plot boundaries, road ribbons with dotted casing, per-field hatch with per-polygon angle, and a town silhouette that is literally the sawtooth union of lot polygons rather than a smoothed hull.

No post in this slice mentions Three.js, WebGL, canvas, seeds, or any renderer/determinism detail. The road-network generation algorithm - the single thing a map generator most needs - is never described; post 84680671 only says 'At this point, the road network is generated.'

Persistence is architecturally load-bearing: descriptions and schedules are baked into the stored settlement (fixes apply 'only for new settlements'), the settlement list and the settlement live in separate stores so population is shown as a derived classification instead of dual-writing, and there is no seed-and-URL reproducibility model at all.
open_questions: How is the road network actually generated? Never described in this slice - no growth model, hierarchy rule, curvature model or seeding strategy. Images show long smooth curving rural roads and an irregular radial-plus-ring urban network with few dead ends.
How is a lot chosen for claiming (nearest-to-centre, largest-first, random?), and what does 'adjacent lot' mean - sharing a road edge or an intersection?
How is a lot subdivided into plots? Images support a perimeter-strip regime and a banded whole-lot regime, but no method is stated.
How are building footprints synthesised (size by type/lifestyle, and the L/T/U lobe rules)?
What are the 'dense phase' and 'sparse phase', in what order do they run, and what is the full enum of 'Can be placed during dense phase when' / 'Can merge when'?
What is a 'building modifier' as distinct from a 'building material'?

Wall geometry: convex hull, alpha shape or offset of built extent, with how much slack? Tower spacing rule? Are gates real objects that snap roads, given district names like Markgate, Cloth Gate, Soutate, Estpass?
Farmland generation: field subdivision method, crop/fallow assignment, hatch-angle rule, extent vs population, and hedgerow tree placement.
Forests: the Forests checkbox and a 'farmland and forests overhaul' exist, but no forest appears in any image in this slice and no method is given.

Generated (non-manual) water: river paths, coastlines, branching, lake formation, island handling, and how the 'required distance between bridges = 100' constraint is enforced. Units of that 100 are unknown.
Coordinate system and world scale - person heights are in real cm, so a metre scale presumably exists, but it is never stated.
Dependency-graph evaluation order: topological sort, fixed-point iteration or greedy loop? Cycle handling? How ratio rules reconcile with the population target?
Full enum of 'Dependency type' (only 'Per other buildings' was screenshotted).
How districts are seeded on the map so industry clusters sensibly near water/gates/walls.
What the empty-space backfill chooses, and whether backfilled buildings get fully realised people (population drift complaints suggest yes).
The district name-erosion algorithm ('Hamlet Tower' -> 'Hamower') and its probability, plus what counts as a detected landmark.
Renderer technology and the server/client split: generation is clearly server-side, but nothing in this slice names Three.js, canvas, SVG rendering or any tiling/LOD scheme.
Is generation seeded or deterministic at all? No seed appears in any UI or URL here, and the creator's reply about watabou-style URL parameters implies not.
Simulation tick semantics: how people are routed between sub-locations (pathfinding vs teleport), whether travel takes time, and what 'Set Location' does to a schedule.
Event selection: how the 10 candidates are ranked from the relation/faction graph, and the full set of state mutations 'Start event' performs.

techniques.name: Recursive lot subdivision - cut proposal rule
techniques.algorithm_summary: Recursively cut any lot too large for a building with a random cut. Old rule: perpendicular to the longest edge from its midpoint. New (Jul 2025): find the edge nearest the lot centroid, cut from it through the centroid.
techniques.biggest_unknown: The 'too large for a building' area threshold and retry/discard policy on failed cuts.

techniques.name: Reflex (interior) corner pre-cut
techniques.algorithm_summary: Before generic division, cut perpendicular to every interior/concave corner of the lot so the divider receives near-rectangular pieces. Fixes L-shaped and hourglass buildings that wrapped around reflex vertices after the suburb update.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Which incident edge the perpendicular is taken from, and the processing order for multiple reflex corners.

techniques.name: Longest-edge heuristic failure via subdivided collinear edges
techniques.algorithm_summary: Debug plot (133016301 #5) shows a 2x4 lot whose long sides are split into unit segments, so the longest single edge is the short end cap and the cut goes the wrong way. Longest-edge is a broken proxy for extent once edges are subdivided.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Whether FTG welds collinear edges at all, or relies solely on the centroid rule to sidestep this.

techniques.name: Narrow-section and sharp-angle building filters
techniques.algorithm_summary: Cheap post-filters: flag an edge flanked by two near-perpendicular edges whose middle edge is too short (narrow neck); flag too-sharp angles between edges. Explicitly does not catch hourglass shapes.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Numeric thresholds for 'too short', 'close-to-perpendicular' and 'too sharp'.

techniques.name: Legacy split projection with mid-line bend
techniques.algorithm_summary: Pick an outside edge, project a splitting line perpendicular into the lot, intersect with the lot, and if the far intersection is not right-angled, bend the line in the middle so both ends meet their edges at 90 degrees. Causes visible kinked party walls and cross-lot splits.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Where along the source edge the line originates and how the bend point is chosen.

techniques.name: Shrink-then-split with blocking edges (Jul 2026)
techniques.algorithm_summary: Inward-offset (erode) the lot; register the inset border as blocking edges; run the same split, which now terminates on the inset instead of the far frontage. Removes both the mid-line bend and cross-lot coupling; output is near-rectangular.
techniques.biggest_unknown: The offset distance d, what the interior core becomes, and the fallback when the lot is too small to shrink.

techniques.name: Castle district pipeline
techniques.algorithm_summary: Random wall layout -> fit into the castle's district lot -> gatehouse area -> keep and other buildings -> connecting paths -> cliffs/moat -> connector road to the road network -> compute surrounding area -> decorate it. Only generated for king/queen feudal government.
techniques.biggest_unknown: How the wall polygon is randomised and how 'fitting' into an arbitrary lot is solved.

techniques.name: Castle park surround via perimeter path
techniques.algorithm_summary: Create a perimeter path looping around the castle, add further random paths, then decorate the resulting sub-areas with trees and grass. Alternative surrounds: plaza, surrounding buildings, cliff.
techniques.biggest_unknown: How the 'surrounding area' polygon is derived and the full decoration option list.

techniques.name: Moat / cliff / beach bands by polygon offsetting
techniques.algorithm_summary: Moat = outward offset band of the curtain-wall polygon with a thin grass berm between (two successive offsets); cliff = grey offset skirt; beach = constant-width tan band inside the shoreline.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Offset distances and join rules; whether one shared offset primitive serves walls, coasts and perimeters.

techniques.name: Post-processing effect chain
techniques.algorithm_summary: Greyscale, sepia, colour tint, pixellation, dot screen, scanline come from the render library's stock extensions (three.js EffectComposer passes); applied in the interactive 2D map, the 3D mode and PNG export. Panel also exposes MSAA, vignette, an SVG renderer and a 3D toggle.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Pass ordering and whether the 2D map is an orthographic WebGL scene (inferred) rather than canvas2D.

techniques.name: Custom crosshatch shader with noise
techniques.algorithm_summary: Hand-written post-processing shader mapping luminance bands to hatch densities/directions; optional noise makes strokes read as pencil. Water becomes dense cross-hatch, roofs single-direction hatch, roads unhatched.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Hatch frequency/threshold ramp and how the noise is applied (screen-space vs world-space).

techniques.name: Tree areas: render-time scatter instead of stored coordinates
techniques.algorithm_summary: Forests store a polygon that is filled with trees at render time rather than persisting one coordinate per tree (50k trees was ~1MB per settlement and >50k rendered trees collapsed framerate). Tree areas are editable in the layout tools.
techniques.biggest_unknown: How the fill is seeded for stability across loads, and the blue-noise/Poisson parameters.

techniques.name: Hipped roofs as flattened 3D geometry
techniques.algorithm_summary: Roofs render as ridge plus facets radiating from each footprint corner - the straight-skeleton picture - and the render settings expose a 'Building roofs: Flattened 3D' mode, implying real 3D roof solids flattened for the 2D map.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Whether a true straight skeleton is used and what the other roof modes are.

techniques.name: Farmland modes: Farmsteads vs Around perimeter
techniques.algorithm_summary: Around perimeter draws fields only along main outbound roads and around the settlement perimeter (default for hamlets). Farmsteads centres a house in a larger plot with a driveway to the road and gives it residents; some farmhands still commute.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Field sizing/placement rules and how many residents a farmstead generates.

techniques.name: Outside-area field partition with hedgerows
techniques.algorithm_summary: Full farmland tiles the ring between settlement perimeter and land boundary as a planar partition of straight-edged polygons seamed by roads, with hedgerow trees along shared edges and per-field parallel crop-row hatching at a per-field angle.
techniques.biggest_unknown: The partition algorithm itself and how crop type per field is chosen (random vs economy-driven).

techniques.name: Blurred field edges
techniques.algorithm_summary: Edges that border plain background are feathered into it over ~15-20px while field/field shared edges stay crisp. Hardware-gated by default; toggleable.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Whether it is a per-edge alpha ramp or a blurred mask pass, and the feather width in world units.

techniques.name: Settlement perimeter expand and round
techniques.algorithm_summary: After suburb generation the perimeter is slightly expanded (to read as gardens behind houses) and rounded off; an outward buffer with round joins that preserves concavities between road fingers. Disable-able in suburb settings; costly enough to erase a round of perf work.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Offset distance, corner radius, and why the smoothing is so expensive.

techniques.name: Outside-settlement decorations with connector paths
techniques.algorithm_summary: Ponds (jittered ~10-gon with a shoreline tree ring), copses (clumped point process), stone circles (~11 jittered stones on a circle over a blended clearing), ruins (rectangles of dashed wall with random gaps). Some types auto-generate a path to the road network; farmland/forest generate around them.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Count/size distributions and the path-routing method to the nearest road.

techniques.name: Island generation as a closed one-arm coast curve
techniques.algorithm_summary: Islands reuse the coastline generator plus recent pond/castle code; coast config is identical (rocky/cliffs/beaches presets, manual coast editing) except an island has one 'arm' rather than two. Shapes observed: rounded triangle, elongated lozenge, two-lobed dumbbell.
techniques.biggest_unknown: The actual outline curve construction (noise-warped radial? midpoint displacement?) and roughness parameters.

techniques.name: Ocean vs river classification heuristic
techniques.algorithm_summary: If a significant portion of a water body's boundary touches the map border it is an ocean, otherwise a river; lakes are lumped in with rivers. Drives which decorations (rocks/cliffs/beaches) and which foam strength apply.
techniques.biggest_unknown: What fraction counts as 'significant', and whether lakes are ever distinguished.

techniques.name: Water depth and foam as distance-from-shore fields
techniques.algorithm_summary: Sea grades from pale at the shore to deep offshore over a distance several times the beach width, uniformly into bays; foam is a near-constant-width white band just offshore tracking every coastline wiggle; rivers get a weaker variant. Signature of an SDF or iterated-blur mask, not an outline stroke.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Implementation (SDF vs blur vs per-vertex distance) and the band widths in world units.

techniques.name: Road network as a planar graph; lots recovered by face traversal
techniques.algorithm_summary: The road network is a graph data structure supporting the fill tool. Two intersections sharing a world position aliased and broke district re-roll; fixed by improved intersection snapping plus a server-side repair of all existing settlements.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Snap tolerance and whether lot polygons are ever cached independently of the graph.

techniques.name: Protobuf settlement file with sint32 coordinates
techniques.algorithm_summary: Settlements persist as protobuf. Positions were two int32; because the map is centred on 0,0 about half are negative and int32 varints encode negatives badly, so switching to sint32 (zig-zag) cut file size ~5%. Simulation reads people straight out of the settlement file.
techniques.biggest_unknown: The rest of the schema and how much of the map is stored vs regenerated on load.

techniques.name: On-demand rendering (no idle frame loop)
techniques.algorithm_summary: Maps render only when the user interacts, to conserve device resources; this forecloses animated water/effects by design. Metropolis render ~10s (was ~20s), with a progressive draw shown during load.
techniques.biggest_unknown: What triggers invalidation and how the progressive draw is staged.

techniques.name: Day/night, weather and season model
techniques.algorithm_summary: Sun moves hourly, changing shadow direction and light brightness/colour; hemisphere and sunrise-direction control shadow orientation; season supplies sunrise/sunset defaults (winter: 8/16, max sun height Low). Weather is a 2x2 of snow-coating x cloudy (cloudy disables shadows). Seasons re-skin deciduous trees (autumn hues, winter bare branches) on the same instances.
techniques.biggest_unknown: The sun-position formula and how the light colour ramp is defined across the day.

techniques.name: Window lights driven by simulation state
techniques.algorithm_summary: At night only buildings containing an awake adult show a lit window - the renderer reads the per-hour population simulation.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Per-hour awake/asleep scheduling rules for the population.

techniques.name: Climate presets with biome-dependent agriculture
techniques.algorithm_summary: Temperate (deciduous/coniferous/mix), desert (sand ground, palms, fields around the perimeter unless a river exists, in which case fields hug the river) and polar (permanent snow, no trees unless forests requested). Conifers ignore seasons and go white in snow.
techniques.biggest_unknown: How far the biome must satisfy the food supply chain, which the creator names as the gating constraint for new climates.

techniques.name: District name generation with syllable budget
techniques.algorithm_summary: Names are assembled from weighted tables of name parts; each part now carries an encoded syllable count so nicknames are capped at 3 syllables for readability.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Table structure, part roles, and the assembly grammar.

techniques.name: User-definable map layers with matchers
techniques.algorithm_summary: Each layer entry has a hex colour plus one or more matchers of type building type / specific building type / specific building. Layers are per-settlement; defaults are configurable pre-generation and travel with saved settings. Activating a thematic layer desaturates the base map and shows a legend card.
techniques.biggest_unknown: The full building-type taxonomy behind the matchers.

techniques.name: Race relations matrix and gender partner weights
techniques.algorithm_summary: A pairwise proportion slider per race pair (9 races -> 45 pairs, default same-race 100, cross-race 0) governs partnering, and can create races with no children/parents. Separately, each person is assigned a preferred partner gender drawn from a weighted config at generation time.
techniques.biggest_unknown: How the proportions are consumed when actually pairing a population.

techniques.name: Faction roles with member criteria and merging
techniques.algorithm_summary: Arbitrary named roles each with a headcount limit and AND-ed criteria over professions, races, genders and religions, plus an 'only people who work at faction buildings' toggle. Same-named roles with different requirements merge after generation.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Selection order when candidates are scarce, and how the building's own job count is reconciled with the faction limit.

techniques.name: Building interiors: room splitting with windows and doors
techniques.algorithm_summary: Early prototype: recursive slicing/BSP of the footprint in its own (non-axis-aligned) frame into ~8 rooms with full-span internal walls; windows are short gaps in exterior walls, doorways are gaps in walls, entrance drawn with a threshold glyph. No furniture or textures yet.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Split-axis choice, minimum room size, and how door-graph reachability is guaranteed.

techniques.name: Grid overlay and measurement units
techniques.algorithm_summary: Unit toggle metres/feet drives grid pitch (2x2 m or 5x5 ft) and the scale bar/ruler; grid cycles off -> light -> dark -> off; at low zoom thin lines are culled and the grid degrades.
techniques.biggest_unknown: World-units-per-metre and how the grid is anchored to the map origin.

top_insights: Buildings come from recursive stochastic subdivision of road-graph lots, and FTG rewrote the cut rule twice in this slice: Jul 2025 replaced 'perpendicular to the longest edge from its midpoint' with 'from the edge nearest the centroid, through the centroid' plus a reflex-corner pre-cut; Jul 2026 replaced the bending cross-lot projection with an inward polygon offset whose inset border acts as blocking edges.

The longest-edge rule fails for a reason worth copying into any design: once an edge has been subdivided by neighbouring cuts, edge length stops being a proxy for extent. The debug plot in 133016301 shows a 2x4 lot cut the wrong way because its long sides were four unit segments.

One randomised closed-outline primitive is reused for ponds, coastlines, islands and castle moats - Thomas says islands were easy because the code already existed from coastline plus recent pond/castle work; an island is the coast curve with one 'arm' instead of two.

Storage cost per settlement is a first-order design constraint because FTG is server-hosted: 50k trees was ~1MB, which forced forests from per-tree coordinates to a stored polygon filled with trees at render time; coordinates were later re-encoded int32 -> sint32 for another 5%.
Rendering is on-demand, never an idle 60fps loop, to conserve device resources - an explicit trade that permanently forecloses animated water or effects and requires disciplined invalidation.

Lot polygons are recovered from the road graph by face traversal, not stored: a single pair of intersections sharing a world position silently disabled the district re-roll/fill tools until snapping was fixed and all existing settlements were repaired server-side.

The simulation gates the map generator: new biomes are blocked on 'keeping the supply chain happy' (how does a desert town with no river get food), window lights only appear for buildings containing an awake adult, and farmsteads create residents who are distinct from commuting farmhands.

Every generated feature grows a manual counterpart (draw water, draw districts, regenerate area, bulk-edit buildings, edit tree areas, custom layers), and invalid input is blocked at the authoring UI rather than tolerated downstream - the geometry assumes simple polygons throughout.
