techniques.name: Tag system / map templates
techniques.algorithm_summary: Closed vocabulary of string tags in URL (?seed=N&tags=a,b,c). Water: coast/river/island/pond/confluence/estuary. Roads: exactly one of highway|dead end|isolated always active, plus crossroads. Also grove, uncultivated, sparse, dense, district, palisade. Tags compose permissively; unsupported combos (palisade+water) allowed but unpolished rather than rejected.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Prior distribution over tags when user requests none; which water tags are mutually exclusive

techniques.name: Ponds
techniques.algorithm_summary: Tag 'pond': usually 1 round pond near map centre, sometimes 2-3, sometimes irregular. Large off-centre pond reads as a lake edge/fjord. Piers explicitly never spawn on ponds. Outline appears to be a near-circle with 3-4 low-amplitude radial harmonics (convex, no pinch-offs).
techniques.biggest_unknown: Radius distribution and the round-vs-irregular decision rule

techniques.name: Meandering rivers
techniques.algorithm_summary: River code fully rewritten in 1.5.2. Rivers now turn >1x per map; this REQUIRED narrowing them (previously up to half map width) because a wide channel can't turn inside a small map. Degenerate cases: near-straight, or one very large turn. Centreline is smooth curve through few control points with alternating lateral offsets, thickened to a ribbon; not a migration simulation (no oxbows, no point-bar asymmetry).
techniques.biggest_unknown: Centreline representation (spline vs subdivision vs smoothed walk) and width distribution

techniques.name: Relief follows rivers
techniques.algorithm_summary: Height field is built AFTER and FROM the water geometry, not sampled independently: 'rivers follow relief... it's the other way around: relief follows rivers'. Kills the glitch of contours running into water. Likely h(p)=base(p)+f(distance_to_water(p)) with f(0)=0 increasing — a distance-transform valley; contours then parallel the bank for free.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Whether height field is grid or analytic, and the valley profile function

techniques.name: Coves and headlands coastline
techniques.algorithm_summary: 1.5.3 replaced straight/broken coasts with coves (concave, common) and headlands (convex, rarer); straight shores remain as the degenerate zero-curvature case. One dominant curvature per map plus a low-amplitude noise octave. Close kin to MFCG's older 'rough parabola' shoreline with randomised sign.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Whether cove/headland is a discrete flag or a signed continuous curvature parameter

techniques.name: Confluence
techniques.algorithm_summary: Two river arms merge at a junction node; village occupies the wedge of land between the arms, downstream of the junction. Arms have independent widths and meander phases; merged channel is wider than either — consistent with three ribbons stitched at a node. Known shipped defect: bridges near confluences cross at wrong angles, because the right-angle rule needs a local channel direction that is ambiguous at the junction.
techniques.biggest_unknown: How the settlement wedge is chosen among the three land regions a Y-junction creates

techniques.name: Estuary as composition
techniques.algorithm_summary: 'Mechanically, an estuary is a combination of a regular river and a bay' — literally the composition of two existing generators, not new geometry. Union of the two water masks with a single shoreline extraction over the union (no seam visible where river ribbon meets bay).
techniques.biggest_unknown: Whether the bay reuses the coast shoreline generator

techniques.name: Bridges
techniques.algorithm_summary: Primary (highway, wide) and secondary (narrower, simpler) bridges; multiple per map allowed; crossing angle 'always as right as possible'; deck casts a shadow band on the water. Right-angling appears to be achieved by choosing the crossing POINT at the locally straightest reach, not by rotating the deck — the road bends on the approaches instead.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Max bridge count, minimum spacing, and whether a bridge guarantees road-graph connectivity across banks

techniques.name: Water rendering: nested offset bands
techniques.algorithm_summary: All water is a stack of concentric bands derived from the shoreline, each inset and each darker along a 2-stop ramp. Outer bands are visibly SMOOTHER than the coastline, so it is iterated offset+smoothing (inset delta, then relax/Chaikin, repeat), not a distance-field threshold or blur. Plus a sand bank strip on the land side and a thin surf stroke. Band count scales with body size (~10 tight bands on a pond, 3-4 wide on open sea). Ramp direction is a palette function — duskvol inverts it.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Band count/spacing rule and whether bands are real polygons or a clipped gradient

techniques.name: Farm fields: grouping and sector layout
techniques.algorithm_summary: Fields group together; small villages get fields on one side only; fields often form sectors centred on the village (strongest on maps with no water and no highway); some get curvilinear edges. Author calls the sector look unrealistic but keeps it for looks. A field group is an annular sector subdivided by narrow access lanes (lanes meet at T-junctions, cells are quads with arc edges) — recursive bisection of a sector, not Voronoi or strips.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Field count rule from population and priority order against woods/water

techniques.name: Furrows
techniques.algorithm_summary: Parallel hatch clipped to the field polygon, constant angle per field, differing between adjacent fields, constant screen spacing. Straight until 1.5.2; 'slightly curvilinear' from 1.5.3 (author accepted odd individual fields for a more organic whole). 1.6.8 replaced the furrow colour parameter with a numeric intensity.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Whether furrow angle is random per field or aligned to the field's OBB; the warp function

techniques.name: Orchards
techniques.algorithm_summary: A field-shaped polygon whose fill is a regular rectangular GRID of individual tree crowns instead of a furrow hatch — same container, different renderer. Enumerated alongside fields by the author ('small fields or orchards inside the palisade'), so handled by the same field-cutting machinery.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Grid spacing rule and the probability a field becomes an orchard

techniques.name: Tree glyph: concentric bands with vertical offset
techniques.algorithm_summary: 'Individual trees are drawn as sets of concentric bands'; from 1.5.3 the bands carry a slight VERTICAL offset, different per tree type, for fake 3D (most visible on cotton). Types: conifer (irregular star), palm (thick bent spikes), cotton (bumpy circle), plus a lobed/maple silhouette. Per-crown colour variation from a small ramp.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Band count per type, offset magnitudes, and whether silhouettes are per-instance or from a prebuilt set

techniques.name: Tree density: warped fractal noise
techniques.algorithm_summary: Density = fBm with DOMAIN WARPING (added 1.5.1 to make wood edges chaotic), modulated by a term that grows trees away from houses and busy roads. Tag 'grove' reverses this so trees hug buildings while map edges are left empty. Trees then sampled by rejection with minimum separation (Poisson-disc-like). Hedgerows along field/river boundaries emerge from the avoidance term, not an explicit feature — the seams between land uses are the surviving density maxima.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Octaves, warp amplitude, avoidance falloff shape; whether grove flips sign or adds an edge penalty

techniques.name: Woods: thicket fill plus boundary crowns
techniques.algorithm_summary: Three LODs for vegetation: (1) individual crowns along the group boundary and scattered inside, (2) a flat fill of the group silhouette in the 'Thicket' colour (parameter added 1.5.4, ported from Cave/Glade Generator), (3) far-field distant woods as a flat tint bounded by a scalloped cloud line with no crowns at all. Line-art styles drop layer 2 entirely, proving the layers are independent.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Whether the group silhouette is a union of crown discs or an alpha threshold of coverage

techniques.name: Tree shadows
techniques.algorithm_summary: Old universal method: duplicate the crown silhouette at a small offset. 1.5.3 changed conifers to a drawn JAGGED TRIANGLE (much better). 2025 improved cotton: the group's shadow is drawn once as a merged union of offset crowns, so overlapping shadows no longer darken cumulatively. Direction and length are global style parameters (shadow angle, shadow length) — SE in most maps, SW in others.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Whether the jagged triangle derives from the crown's spikes or is generated fresh; shadow colour derivation

techniques.name: Tree gradients and group shading
techniques.algorithm_summary: Three independent layers, provable from a same-seed 3-panel comparison: (a) group-level shading across the whole wood silhouette (1.6.2, strength tied to shadow color AND shadow length), (b) per-crown gradient with options None/Linear/Radial (1.6.7, ported from Cave/Glade and Urban Places), (c) cast shadow. Trees dialog also holds Zero/Random/Maximum tree counts.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Gradient stop colours and whether the linear direction equals the light azimuth

techniques.name: Road merging
techniques.algorithm_summary: 1.5.4: roads merge tangentially into each other (rounded Y-junctions with a fillet) instead of butting in as square T-junctions. Author calls the implementation 'quite crude' and places the toggle in the Style dialog, which elsewhere holds only appearance parameters — so most likely a junction-RENDERING treatment on the road ribbon rather than a road-graph change. Independent of the 1.6.1 orthogonality fix.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Whether it is a graph operation or purely a rendering fillet

techniques.name: Driveways
techniques.algorithm_summary: Short perpendicular stubs in the road colour connecting SOME buildings (mostly larger ones) to the road they line. Connecting ALL buildings was tried and rejected because it 'looked wrong, like modern suburbia' — partial connectivity IS the feature. Toggle lives in Layers, not Style. Selection is probably a probability weighted by footprint area, since both small and large buildings get stubs.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Exact selection probability and stub length rule

techniques.name: Isohypse-preferring road routing
techniques.algorithm_summary: 1.5.4: roads run uphill/downhill 'more reluctantly', preferring isohypses as a function of slope steepness. Implies a least-cost path whose edge weight includes a gradient term, e.g. len*(1+k*|dh|/len), since the penalty is itself slope-dependent. Author is openly unsure the result looks better. Hairpins/serpentines deliberately NOT implemented — current slopes are too gentle to need them, and this is a stated prerequisite for cliffs.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Cost function shape and whether the search runs on a grid or on candidate segments

techniques.name: Population density map
techniques.algorithm_summary: One scalar field with at least three consumers: spotlight focus (default = point of maximum density), palisade enclosure shape (sparse villages get smaller fences, dense get larger radius), and building placement density. Exposed via dense/sparse/district tags. Regenerated 'very differently' in 1.6.1, which also fixed unreasonably curvy roads — the two are linked because road routing consumes the field, so small-scale noise made paths wander on flat ground. This is a same-seed behaviour shift.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Its actual form before or after the 1.6.1 rewrite — the single largest gap in the slice

techniques.name: Palisades
techniques.algorithm_summary: Village generated FIRST, wall second: enclosure derived from the population density map (almost certainly a smoothed level set — the loops are C1-smooth, convex-ish, slightly irregular ovals). The fence cuts through woods with a chance to leave trees inside, and cuts fields the same way (this path is 'much more complex and more glitchy', fields commonly overlap — a shipped known defect). Gates are NOT real gates: ordinary houses placed where roads cross the wall, which is why they can be numbered and opened in Dwellings. Rendered as a dense row of small circles (stake tops) at fixed arclength along a continuous darker band, with a cleared strip just inside. Exported as 'just another list of polylines', deliberately NOT as a city wall.
techniques.biggest_unknown: How the level threshold is chosen, and the parameterisation of 'chance to leave trees inside'

techniques.name: Village square and centrepieces
techniques.algorithm_summary: Round squares more common than rectangular, deliberately ('round squares look more natural'). Centrepiece variants observed: dot/well, tower (a square building distinguished purely by a LONGER shadow), a single tree, a dome on a large flat-roofed building (circle filled with a spiral of concentric arcs), or nothing. When the square overlaps a highway they are always ALIGNED to stop the highway entering at an oblique angle. Towers were props until 1.6.5 made them real buildings.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Round/rectangular probability split, centrepiece selection rule, and whether the square moves after highway routing

techniques.name: Roof styles and house rendering
techniques.algorithm_summary: Four styles: gable (ridge along long axis, hatch perpendicular, one slope lighter; 'still the most polished'), hip (corner diagonals to a short ridge, four toned facets), flat (plain rectangle, doubled inset outline, inner shadow from 1.5.4; large flat-roofed buildings get a DOME instead of a tower), ruin (no roof, incomplete wall set). Per-building roof colour from a small palette. 1.6.8 replaced hatching colour with a numeric Details parameter (0 hides hatching, 1 makes it prominent).
techniques.biggest_unknown: Roof-style selection rule per building and the size threshold for dome-bearing buildings

techniques.name: Fake perspective and Top-down option
techniques.algorithm_summary: Houses are oblique extrusions with a GLOBALLY CONSTANT extrusion vector (not per-building, not radial from map centre): base rectangle, roof = base offset by a constant vector, side quads between them, plus a separate cast shadow whose direction is independent of the extrusion. Trees use the same trick via their per-type vertical band offset. 1.6.7 added a 'Top-down' toggle disabling it on houses and trees, planned to become default and then permanent. Crucially, the author states that better/non-rectangular buildings REQUIRE abandoning fake perspective — rectangularity is a consequence of this renderer.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Extrusion height as a function of building size and roof style

techniques.name: Spotlight
techniques.algorithm_summary: Full-frame soft radial gradient composited over the finished map (it affects land AND water, so it is not baked into the ground fill). Focus defaults to the point of maximum population density; alternatives are map centre or pushed to the edge per shadow angle. Periphery darkened with the shadow colour, focus highlighted with its COMPLEMENT; only saturation is user-adjustable; darkening and lightening intensities independent; a size parameter; key L. Stated purpose: fight the monotony of empty space — 'an empty patch of a subtle gradient looks better than an empty patch of solid colour'.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Which blend operators implement the darken/lighten pair

techniques.name: Ground shading (hillshade)
techniques.algorithm_summary: 1.6.2: sun-facing slopes highlighted, opposite darkened. Functionally duplicates hachures but ALSO affects roads and fields (applied to the whole ground stack above fields/roads, below trees/houses; water appears exempt). Strength tied to shadow color; at extremes the ground looks 'plastic'. Standard Lambert shade from the height gradient using the same light azimuth as the cast shadows.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Exact shade-to-colour mapping and whether water is genuinely exempt

techniques.name: Relief modes: hachures, contours, grass
techniques.algorithm_summary: Three renderers over the same iso-line extraction: continuous wavy lines (Contours), rows of tiny dashes laid along the contours forming nested loops around hills (Hachures), and jittered tick marks (Grass, reworked in 1.6.7 into 'noisier hachures'; author doubts it is needed). Plausibly the same nested-offset machinery as the water bands. Cliffs — described in 2023 as 'not real, just fancy contour lines' — remain unimplemented through 1.6.8, blocked on making roads and houses interact with them.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Contour interval rule and the tick-placement/jitter parameters

techniques.name: Selective outlining and Pressure
techniques.algorithm_summary: 1.6.8: outlines drawn in shades of the objects themselves rather than solid black/Ink ('selective outlining'). New Pressure parameter controls how much Ink affects the final outline colour, mixed with HARD LIGHT blend mode. Pressure=1.0 is a discontinuous special case reverting to solid Ink ('1 and 0.999 may produce very different results'); Pressure=0 disables all outlines and most strokes (key P). Same-seed before/after shows the black shoreline disappearing and each object class taking a darker shade of its own fill. Simultaneously, roof hatching / tree detail / furrow COLOUR parameters became numeric intensities.
techniques.biggest_unknown: The darkening function applied to the fill before the Hard Light mix, and why 1.0 is discontinuous

techniques.name: Village lights from a continuous map
techniques.algorithm_summary: 1.6.8: lights switch on/off 'based on a single continuous map' rather than independently, so some streets are busy and others quiet. Converts an i.i.d. per-lamp Bernoulli into spatially correlated on/off runs — a smooth scalar field (plausibly the density map or low-frequency noise) sampled per lamp and thresholded. 1.6.4 had already made lights brighter but less 'blinding' so they stop obscuring detail below.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Whether the continuous map is the population density field or a separate noise field

techniques.name: House numbering order
techniques.algorithm_summary: Started as a debug feature, repurposed after feedback to allow numbering a subset (shift+click or context menu). On a 133-building map the order starts at the village core, walks outward in contiguous runs ALONG streets, and ends with a trailing block of scattered peripheral buildings — neither a spatial sort nor a spiral. Best explanation: it is the internal creation order of the building list (centre-out, street-by-street, with an outskirts pass appended), which matches the author calling it 'interesting, but maybe not the most convenient'.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Whether the outskirts pass is a genuinely separate stage and how it differs from the main pass

techniques.name: JSON export and City Viewer
techniques.algorithm_summary: Palisade exported as 'just another list of polylines' — the author explicitly refused to reuse the existing city-wall channel because it would look weird in City Viewer. Viewer renders palisades as smooth extruded low walls, gates as ordinary gabled houses straddling them, the square as a flat ellipse with a small cylinder, buildings as white boxes with brown gable roofs, trees as green ellipsoids, fields as flat polygons. Permalinks encode seed+tags and, from 1.6.5, which buildings are numbered.
techniques.biggest_unknown: The full JSON schema and the geometry type used for palisade polylines

techniques.name: MFCG size parameter semantics
techniques.algorithm_summary: From a comment reply: the 'size' parameter determines the number of CELLS, each cell divided into blocks and then individual buildings — it is not a building count. A medium city is usually 1000-2000 buildings, with the exact number shown in the Settlement window. Explains why building counts vary at a fixed size setting.
techniques.biggest_unknown: The cell-to-block-to-building fan-out distribution

top_insights: Relief is derived FROM water, not independently: 'rivers follow relief... it's the other way around: relief follows rivers'. The height field is built after the water mask, which is why contours parallel banks and never run into water.

One population-density scalar field drives spotlight focus, palisade shape, building density and (indirectly) road curvature. It was regenerated 'very differently' in 1.6.1, which simultaneously fixed 'unreasonably curvy roads' — a same-seed behaviour shift and the slice's biggest reproduction gap.

Water, hills and palisades all use one geometric idiom: nested offset loops of a region boundary with per-step smoothing. Outer water bands are visibly smoother than the coastline, which rules out distance-field thresholds and blurs.
Meander amplitude and river width are coupled — the author had to narrow rivers a lot before they could meander, and accepted losing piers on narrow rivers as the price.

Several signature features are deliberate anti-realism: sector-shaped fields ('probably not very realistic... but it looks nice'), palisades cutting woods with trees left inside ('doesn't make much sense, but it looks more interesting'), and driveways on only some buildings because connecting all 'looked wrong, like modern suburbia'.

Tree crowns are concentric bands with a per-type vertical offset; the wood is a separate flat 'thicket' fill under boundary crowns; far-field woods are a flat tint with a scalloped edge. Three independent layers, provable because line-art styles drop the middle one.

Palisade gates are not gates — they are ordinary houses placed where roads cross the wall, which is exactly why they can be numbered and opened in Dwellings while 'towers' could not until they too became real buildings.

Fake perspective is a known dead end the author intends to abandon: non-rectangular, more varied houses are stated to require dropping it, and a Top-down toggle was shipped in 1.6.7 on a path to becoming permanent.

Selective outlining (1.6.8) replaces black outlines with darker shades of each object's own fill, mixed with Ink under a Hard Light blend via a 'Pressure' parameter that is discontinuous at 1.0 and has a separate meaning at 0.
VG is not village-scale only: maps in this slice run from Pop. 130 to Pop. 1700, the largest showing a full radial-concentric street web with ring roads and radial spokes.

techniques.name: Population-before-layout invariant
techniques.algorithm_summary: People and the building manifest are generated first; total building area drives how much road network/lot area is grown. Creator: 'I don't see this ever changing.'
techniques.biggest_unknown: The packing factor converting building manifest area into target lot area.

techniques.name: Generation pipeline V1 (pre-overhaul)
techniques.algorithm_summary: 1 people/buildings, 2 split buildings into districts, 3 grow roads until lots total the needed area, 4 each district claims a lot and grows into adjacent ones placing buildings, 5 repeat. Undersized districts get merge logic.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Lot-claim/grow acceptance rules and the retry budget before abort.

techniques.name: V1 failure mode: large-building placement abort
techniques.algorithm_summary: After the map-scale fix shrank typical buildings but not temples/mansions, districts could not fit large buildings in small lots; after N attempts the whole generation gave up. Also caused slowness.
techniques.biggest_unknown: The attempt count and whether retry was per-district or global.

techniques.name: Road growth V1: proposal-queue segment agents
techniques.algorithm_summary: Placed segments propose successors ('continue straight', 'branch left/right at right angles') into a queue; each popped proposal passes validity checks then spawns more. Two phases: dense core, then outer buildings. Always starts at a 4-way crossroad -> circular blob.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Contents of the validity checks and the queue priority order.

techniques.name: Road generation V2: configurable phases
techniques.algorithm_summary: Same agent core, tuned to yield much larger lots handed to districts. Configurable initial junction (3/4/5-way, through-road, ring); N phases each with {ends-in-wall, wiggliness, branching strategy, building-placement mode}.
techniques.biggest_unknown: How 'wiggliness' and each 'branching strategy' are parameterised.

techniques.name: Generation pipeline V2 (shipped Jan 2025)
techniques.algorithm_summary: Categorise buildings into pools; grow main roads until a large lot exists; pick district type from remaining buildings; district places landmarks FIRST while the lot is big, then subdivides and fills; repeat. Districts own their internal road style.
techniques.biggest_unknown: The lot subdivision method itself (OBB bisection? skeleton? road-driven?) — deferred to the user guide.

techniques.name: Suburb generation (ribbon lots, no surrounding roads)
techniques.algorithm_summary: Buildings placed along a road spur without a closed road face; dead-end ribbons radiate from the core so towns grow along main roads instead of as circles. Changed how hamlets/villages generate.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Spur length/spacing distributions and per-building setback rules.

techniques.name: 'Gaps' building placement mode
techniques.algorithm_summary: Dense subdivision, then each footprint is shrunk so buildings do not touch. Now the default outside the settlement centre.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Whether the inset is absolute or proportional, and its value.

techniques.name: Straight-skeleton roofs
techniques.algorithm_summary: Replaces a rectangular roof texture overlay. Straight skeleton of the footprint gives hip roofs for arbitrary (concave, custom-drawn) polygons; gable via extra post-processing. Flattened 2D and full 3D variants; old renderer kept as default on weak devices.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Degeneracy handling and the exact hip-to-gable post-process.

techniques.name: Height map as a separate raster
techniques.algorithm_summary: Perlin/simplex noise into a separate height map at a chosen resolution rather than promoting 2D points to 3D, because a 2-point road segment would have no mid-span height. Potentially lazy-derived from a seed rather than stored.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Noise type/octaves, heightMapWidth, and whether it ever shipped stored or seed-derived.

techniques.name: Lattice re-triangulation of background polygons
techniques.algorithm_summary: PlaneGeometry(mapWidth,mapWidth,heightMapWidth,heightMapWidth) for terrain; texture polygons default-triangulate into slivers with no interior vertices, so they are re-triangulated onto a regular lattice aligned across neighbours to sample height and reduce clipping.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Whether the lattice is truly global/shared or per-polygon with snapping.

techniques.name: Planar partition via Clipper polygon subtraction
techniques.algorithm_summary: Tessellation tuning failed to stop z-fighting between layered ground textures; instead each lower polygon has the upper ones subtracted (js-angusj-clipper), so nothing renders on top of anything. Removes clipping and hidden triangles. Roads still clip slightly; accepted.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Layer ordering rules and why roads are excluded.

techniques.name: Junction disc rendering for roads
techniques.algorithm_summary: Road strokes (body + casing + centre stripe) left a notch at bends; a circle is now drawn at the intersection, sized and coloured from the incident roads, plus the edges. Applies to most drawn lines.
techniques.biggest_unknown: The size/colour rule when roads of different classes meet.

techniques.name: River path tool (centreline -> ribbon)
techniques.algorithm_summary: User draws a polyline path; sliders set River width (125 seen) and Smoothness (3 seen, reads as subdivision iterations); result is a smooth constant-width polygon. Water may not intersect a red exclusion circle at the settlement core.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Smoothing scheme (Chaikin vs spline) and whether width can vary along the path.

techniques.name: Coastline decoration (beaches, cliffs, rocks)
techniques.algorithm_summary: Ocean boundary roughness is controllable; boundary runs are classified as sand/pebble beach, cliff or rock. Beaches render as an inland-offset hatched band; cliffs/rocks as glyph chains along the waterline. Also pushes buildings/farmland back from the water.
techniques.biggest_unknown: How runs are classified and how the buildable area is clipped back.

techniques.name: Harbours in waterfront districts
techniques.algorithm_summary: Generated as part of waterfront districts with options for harbour shape, harbour-wall shape+material, pier shape+material. Images show basins with stone quays, plank/T-head/ladder piers, and rock breakwaters.
techniques.biggest_unknown: How the harbour footprint is fitted to the coast and the basin cut from land/ocean.

techniques.name: Walls as a road-phase terminator
techniques.algorithm_summary: A generation phase can 'end in a wall'. New wall types with stone as default, scalable towers, walls split across rivers. Rendered as a constant-width band with rounded corners and an internal ring road; encloses only the old town in big cities.
techniques.biggest_unknown: How the wall polyline is derived and tower spacing/gate placement.

techniques.name: Family-unit relation normalisation
techniques.algorithm_summary: Replaced pairwise person-person edges (6 per family of 4) with one family-unit object {parents, children} plus pointers; derivable relations (siblings) are not persisted. Relations fell from ~30% to ~10% of settlement file size, enabling 50k settlements.
techniques.biggest_unknown: How remarriage/step-relations are modelled and whether a person holds two unit pointers.

techniques.name: Schedule model and profession templates
techniques.algorithm_summary: Schedule = day-sets (relevant days 1/7..7/7) x hourly time ranges, each with a status, a primary-behaviour criterion, and primary/default behaviours resolving to {action, building matcher, sub-location matcher, exact sub-location}. Schedules can now be auto-filled from a preconfigured job.

techniques.name: Map scale correction (3x bug) and ruler
techniques.algorithm_summary: x/y were not 1:1 with metres (only z was), making buildings ~3x too large. A ruler tool was built to diagnose it and then shipped as a feature. Re-tuning sizes to real-world dimensions broke placement reliability and triggered the V2 rewrite.

techniques.name: Arced map labels
techniques.algorithm_summary: Settlement/district names set in cream small-caps serif with heavy black outline plus shadow, bent along a shallow arc following the district's principal axis, sized by importance.
techniques.biggest_unknown: How the arc and font size are fitted to the district polygon.

techniques.name: Farmland and forest rendering
techniques.algorithm_summary: Countryside is a gapless polygonal partition of quadrilateral fields in 4 crop fills, each with fine hatching along its own axis, hedgerow trees on boundaries. Forests are a green base plus a dense field of scribble glyphs thinning at the edge.

techniques.name: Tiered rendering and web workers
techniques.algorithm_summary: Expensive features ship with a cheaper fallback selected by device power (old vs skeleton roofs; flattened vs 3D). Jan 2025 added more web workers for the building render step; generation ~10% faster after the overhaul.

top_insights: The whole 2024-06 to 2025-01 rewrite has one root cause: fixing a 3x map-scale bug shrank typical buildings but not temples/mansions, so the large-building:lot-area ratio blew up and the placement search started aborting. Scale, lot size and landmark size are a single coupled invariant.

V2 inverts control: V1 grew a global road mesh, cut small lots, placed buildings, then merged lots into districts (hence mixed-purpose and disconnected districts). V2 grows coarse LARGE lots, hands each to a district, and the district places landmarks first, then subdivides and fills — so road style becomes a district property.

Landmark-first placement is the reliability fix: place the hard (largest) object while the lot is still big and unconstrained, then generate roads around it. That converts a failing search into a trivially satisfiable one.

People and buildings are generated BEFORE the layout, permanently ('I don't see this ever changing'). The map is a fitting problem for a known building manifest, not a landscape that is later populated.

Clipper polygon subtraction, not tessellation tuning, is what makes layered ground textures work: subtract upper layers from lower ones to get a planar partition where nothing overlaps — fixes z-fighting and cuts hidden triangles at the same time. The same offsetting library almost certainly powers rivers, quays, walls and the 'gaps' inset.

Height is stored as a separate raster, deliberately, because a road segment is only two points and would get no mid-span height; a raster can also be lazily regenerated from a seed instead of stored per settlement.

Straight skeleton is the roof primitive: hip roofs fall out directly for arbitrary concave footprints, gable is a post-process — and the flattened 2D variant is what gives FTG's top-down buildings their two-tone roof-facet look.
Suburb ribbons (buildings along a spur with no closed road face) are what broke the 'circular blob' signature; towns now grow anisotropically along main roads and fray into starfish outlines.

The old algorithm's signature was structural, not stylistic: every town started at a 4-way crossroad and bloomed circularly because segment agents only proposed 'straight ahead' and 'branch at right angles'. Configurable initial junctions and per-phase branching strategies are the cure.

The simulation is a deterministic query over schedules, not a stepped agent sim: hour-granularity day-set schedules with primary/default behaviour resolution, which is why arbitrary time skips and hourly external calendar sync are cheap.

techniques.name: Core pipeline: height map -> gradient vector field -> "trackers" -> roads
techniques.algorithm_summary: Launch post 35854256 states it verbatim: a height map is created; a gradient vector field is derived from it; a set of 'trackers' (streamline walkers) run through that field and draw the roads; a separate 'density map' decides where roads branch more and where more buildings are placed. Same machinery reused from Procgen Tarot and Winter Trees. 1.3.0's 'organic' tag statement ('forces roads to follow the relief closely; normally they resist the relief trying to stay straight') shows the heading update is a weighted blend of momentum and field direction. Replaces MFCG's subdivision-first approach because MFCG degrades at village scale.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Whether street trackers follow the gradient or the gradient rotated 90 degrees (contour tangent) - every island/hill image shows streets as concentric contour-parallel arcs while the highway crosses contours freely; plus step size, seed count, branch rule and the near-miss snapping that creates closed blocks.

techniques.name: Density map (population-density field)
techniques.algorithm_summary: A second scalar field over the map. Stated consumers: (1) road branching rate, (2) buildings per unit length of road (35854256, 38498864); (3) field cell size, inversely (57968729); (4) the village square is placed at a high-density location, 'often on the highway' (80494491). The UI dial Low/Med/High is a global scale on it; map size scales its spread ('the larger the map, the larger the village spawned on it'). Population is a derived output, not an input - zero-pop villages were to be fixed by regenerating until pop>0.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Construction: number/placement of bumps, the highway ridge term, and whether printed population is the field integral or a building count times household size.

techniques.name: Building placement along road centrelines
techniques.algorithm_summary: All buildings are rectangles (stated, 66544756) with a real stored footprint size. Placement walks each road polyline at arc-length steps scaled by 1/density, offsets by a fixed per-class setback along the normal, orients the long axis along the tangent, and rejects on collision - inferred from MFCG's adoption note (37407181: 'placed more sparsely... but all proper rectangles'), which is the signature of rejection sampling. Street width (house spacing) is explicitly decoupled from stroke width (80494491). The same 'place along a curve with setback' rule is reused for shorelines (port frontage) and for the square's boundary ring.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Whether sides alternate deterministically, the footprint size distribution, and what 'No empty roads' (1.1.0) actually does - delete the road or force a building onto it.

techniques.name: Fields: density-scaled tiling with shape rejection
techniques.algorithm_summary: Stated brief (50688261): mostly rectangular, comfortable aspect ratio, hint at relief, clustered near houses, no croft/field distinction. Tiler is seeded from the highway polyline and water edges ('fields adjoin the main road, but not the smaller streets'), and further from the centre cells line up in circles around it. 1.2.7 rules: at most one house per field or the FIELD is discarded; field size scales inversely with population density so rejects do not punch holes in the patchwork; trails crossing a field are truncated and their terminal house moved to the new endpoint and aligned to the field edge; triangular/sectorial/non-compact fields are discarded. Cells share edges but are inset to leave ground-coloured lanes; furrows run along each cell's long axis and are drawn dashed from 1.2.7.
techniques.biggest_unknown: The actual partition primitive (strip cuts vs recursive OBB split vs polar sectoring), the inset distance, and the numeric thresholds of the compactness/aspect predicate.

techniques.name: Village square: distorted circle at the density maximum
techniques.algorithm_summary: 80494491 verbatim: find a place of high population density (often on the highway), create a circle of 'reasonable size' there, distort it a little; that is the square. If it does not overlap water, add a centrepiece - a large tree or a well. Roughly half of villages get one; 'no square' tag suppresses it. Roads/trails radiate from it and houses ring it tangentially. In 1.5.0 the 'dead end' tag makes the highway terminate at the square.
techniques.biggest_unknown: The size rule ('reasonable size') and the distortion amplitude/spectrum; whether the square seeds new trackers for its radials.

techniques.name: Orchards from house-overlapped fields
techniques.algorithm_summary: 80494491: any field polygon overlapped by one or more houses becomes an orchard, filled with regular rows of smaller trees; if the plot shape is 'particularly irregular', trees are scattered chaotically instead. 'no orchards' tag suppresses generation; orchards can also be hidden separately. This converts the 1.2.5 'houses on fields = crofts' complaint into a feature.
techniques.biggest_unknown: The shape-regularity test that selects rows vs chaos, and the row spacing / crown size relative to wild trees.

techniques.name: Forests: fill-then-carve with clearance around houses and roads
techniques.algorithm_summary: 42521165 comment, verbatim: 'Many trees' = fill the whole map with trees; 'Some trees' = create random patches of trees; then in both cases trees too close to cottages or roads are removed. Proven by Wilderness mode (66544756/04), where hiding the village still leaves a village-shaped clearing, and by lone houses inside their own forest clearings. Tree coverage has its own RNG stream (rerollable with Shift+T without changing the map).
techniques.biggest_unknown: The candidate generator (Poisson-disc? jittered grid?), the patch generator for 'Some', and the clearance radii for houses vs roads vs trails.

techniques.name: Tree drawing methods, ending in "Improved"
techniques.algorithm_summary: Simple (cog-like discs) -> Cotton (fluffy irregular puffs) -> Blobs (merged silhouettes, 'very many inner parameters') -> Improved (1.3.0): of a group of trees the outer ones are drawn normally as cotton trees, those further from the edges are drawn muted, and the interior of the group is a solid colour blob. This resolves the stated dilemma that individual-tree depiction is a large-scale convention and homogeneous-area depiction a small-scale one, while village maps sit at 'an inconvenient middle scale'. All other methods were deleted in 1.4.0. Shapes Cotton/Spiky added 1.5.0; shadows have varying lengths for a natural combined silhouette.
techniques.biggest_unknown: The rim/muted/interior band widths and how group boundaries are computed from the tree point set.

techniques.name: Relief: marks stamped along evenly-resampled isolines
techniques.algorithm_summary: 71653886 verbatim: hachures, Grass (zigzags) and Contours 'really just draw shapes along isolines. Isolines themselves are now built more evenly across a map, preventing hachures from overlapping.' Hachures are short perpendicular strokes in two tones (hachureLight/hachureDark) giving a shaded-relief read; Grass replaces them with zigzags; Contours draws the isoline itself. Introduced 1.2.0 as 'something (but not exactly) like hachures'; evened out in 1.2.7 and again in 1.3.0; per-style, disableable, absent from Minimalist.
techniques.biggest_unknown: How isolines are extracted (marching squares vs analytic) and what 'built more evenly across a map' does concretely - that step is the difference between good hachures and clumped ones.

techniques.name: Water: coast / river / island, and the 'earth bounds' land polygon
techniques.algorithm_summary: 1.1.0 added coast and river ('especially rivers' were hard); 1.2.2 added islands; 1.2.5 made all three shapes more diverse and rivers narrower and more meandering. Critically, in 1.1.0 'the water and the potential village area are created independently', causing villages detached from their own coast. The 1.2.5 'fields only on one bank of a river' bug was diagnosed a release later as a bug in 'the method I used to calculate earth bounds' - i.e. there is an explicit land polygon and it was computed as one connected region. Render: deep fill + shallow band(s) + waterTide ripple contours + sand beach; N-band gradient from 1.4.0; white thalweg line on rivers.
techniques.biggest_unknown: The shape generator for all three water configurations is completely undocumented, as is how 'more meandering' rivers were achieved and whether rivers relate to the height field at all.

techniques.name: Ports: piers and shore frontage
techniques.algorithm_summary: 38498864: 'If a layout allows, some piers are placed within a village's border and connected with the rest of the village... Besides piers, port areas are also populated by buildings along the shore.' Piers are roads that end in water. 1.2.5 fixed several dock bugs - piers intersecting each other or ending on land - via pairwise-intersection and end-in-water validation, but 'they still get spawned at odd locations'. Watermills are deliberately NOT generated: the plan is to tag suitable existing buildings as such.
techniques.biggest_unknown: What 'if a layout allows' means precisely, and the location-quality predicate that was never solved.

techniques.name: Road hierarchy, junction style and highway topology tags
techniques.algorithm_summary: Four render classes: highway (widest ribbon, crosses the map), secondary streets, lanes, and dashed trails. 1.2.7: 'fewer crossroads, more T-junctions, and newly introduced right angle turns... makes villages more compact and less regular' - inferred as a junction-resolution rule (terminate on, or snap to 90 degrees against, an existing road) rather than a new growth rule. 1.4.0 decoupled per-class stroke thickness from the geometric street width used to space houses. 1.5.0 tags: 'isolated' (no highway at all) and 'dead end' (highway terminates at the square); two intersecting highways (crossroads) was attempted and abandoned as harder than expected.
techniques.biggest_unknown: How the highway's path and its map-border entry/exit are chosen, and why multi-highway topology is hard in this model.

techniques.name: 'Lonely houses' as a tuned emergent artefact
techniques.algorithm_summary: 57968729: isolated houses outside the village connected by a trail were 'not something I planned, but more like a byproduct of other processes'. Kept because they read as farmsteads, then tuned distributionally rather than structurally: fewer trails spawned, and each made longer on average so its endpoint more often falls outside the map rectangle, where the house is culled.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Trail length distribution and spawn count relative to village size.

techniques.name: Palette / style data model (17-slot Vivid schema, per-style schemas)
techniques.algorithm_summary: Eight real palette files were attached to post 42521165 (mis-saved as .jpg) and are transcribed verbatim in the findings file. Vivid schema: ground, hachureLight/Dark, roofLight/Dark, sand, ink, waterShallow/Deep/Tide, forestLight/Dark, lights, shadowAlpha, strokeNormal/Thin, roofVariance. Calligraphy, Minimalist and Scribble had completely different, smaller schemas (white/light/dark/black + four stroke weights; paper/ink/water/forest/road + forestAlpha; paper/ink/water/forest + two strokes) - proving the early 'styles' were separate renderers, which is why three of the four were deleted in 1.2.3. Later slots: Planks, Shadow{Colour,Length,Angle}, Paper (text outlining), roof-hatching colour, Slope, No. of bands, outlining none/hard/soft, Roof type, Tree shape.

techniques.name: Roof rendering: single colour x shadow, multi-colour, faked perspective, gable/hip
techniques.algorithm_summary: 1.3.0: only one roof colour is required; the unlit face is computed by multiplying it by the shadow colour. Multiple roof colours may be assigned per village; roof hatching gets its own colour so it can be muted or hidden; and roofs are drawn 'faking perspective or angled top-down view' controlled by a Slope parameter. 1.5.0 adds Roof type Gable/Hip (flat considered). roofVariance ('Color variance', default 0.2) jitters each building's roof colour.

techniques.algorithm_summary: Creator comment on 84106820: small/medium/large map sides are exactly 300 / 500 / 800 generator units; JSON export converts 1 unit to 0.7 metres, making a medium map 350x350 m. Default size became 'medium' in 1.3.0 ('formerly known as small'). Non-square maps arrived in 1.5.0 with free width/height fields; map rotation was removed in 1.3.0 precisely to enable them.

techniques.name: Determinism, permalinks and cross-generator integration
techniques.algorithm_summary: Permalinks (56941736) took 5 days and make the whole map reconstructible from a URL - strong evidence generation is a pure function of (seed, parameters). Perilous Shores passes a settlement into VG preserving its name and water configuration; Procgen Mansion receives a clicked building's dimensions (VG footprints are plain rectangles, which made PM plans boring, so PM was allowed more intricate plans); City Viewer consumes the JSON. JSON deliberately left strict GeoJSON for a 'GeoJSON-like' format; height maps are NOT exported, so 3D views render on a flat plane; fields were added to the export in 1.2.5.

techniques.name: POI generation (content exists, annotation unsolved)
techniques.algorithm_summary: POI naming and typing existed internally from 1.2.2 onward and printed to the browser console (examples given: "Arnald's Blades (smithy)", "The Cup And Arrow (tavern)"). The feature never shipped in this window because of a purely cartographic blocker: no room for a legend, the creator is 'sick and tired of implementing the legend in my every generator', wants everything on a single printed page, and PS-style stickers 'looked wrong'. top_insights: The launch post (35854256) states VG's entire core algorithm in one paragraph - height map, gradient vector field, 'trackers' that draw roads, and a separate 'density map' driving branching and building counts. This closes two questions the sibling slice vg-ng-devlogs.md reported as UNKNOWN, and it means VG is road-first/field-driven, architecturally unrelated to MFCG's subdivision-first approach.

Post 42521165's eight 'images' 03-10.jpg are not images: they are the actual VG palette JSON files, giving the complete 17-slot Vivid style schema with real hex values, plus three entirely different schemas for the Calligraphy, Minimalist and Scribble styles - proving those early 'styles' were separate renderers, which explains why three of the four were deleted in 1.2.3.

The single most transferable design trick in the slice is 1.2.7's field sizing: make fields smaller where population density is higher, so that discarding invalid fields does not leave visible holes in the patchwork. Shrink the rejection unit wherever rejection is likely.

Forests are generated fill-then-carve: fill the map (or random patches) with trees, then delete every tree too close to a house or road. Wilderness mode proves the carve is baked at generation time - hiding the village still leaves a village-shaped clearing in the wood.

All three relief styles (hachures, grass zigzags, contours) are one mechanism: stamp marks along evenly-resampled isolines of the height field. The recurring bug and the recurring fix were both about isoline spacing, not about the marks.

Roads normally 'resist the relief trying to stay straight' and the 'organic' tag raises the field weight - so the tracker heading is a blend of momentum and field direction, with one exposed knob. But the images show streets running along contours while the highway crosses them, which the stated 'gradient field' wording does not explain; this is the biggest reproduction gap.

Exact scale constants exist: map sides are 300 / 500 / 800 generator units and JSON export uses 1 unit = 0.7 m, making a medium map 350 x 350 m. That pins house footprints at roughly 10 x 5 m, which cross-validates the constant.

Two failure-handling patterns recur and are worth copying: retry-the-whole-map for global failures (zero-population villages), and repair-the-dependent for local ones (a trail clipped by a field has its terminal house moved to the new endpoint and re-aligned to the field's edge).

The creator's hardest unsolved problem is not geometry but annotation: POI content (named taverns, smithies) has existed since 1.2.2 and still only prints to the browser console, blocked entirely by 'everything must fit on one printed page' plus legend fatigue.

Rendering, not generation, is the performance bottleneck. By 1.2.8 generation was 'quite fast' while drawing was not, and trees were the dominant cost across three years - they shipped disabled by default for over a year.
open_questions: Do village-street trackers follow the gradient or the contour-tangent (gradient rotated 90 degrees)? Images say contour for streets and free crossing for the highway; the only statement says 'gradient vector field'.

Tracker parameters: step size, seed count and placement, branch probability formula, termination rule, and the near-miss snapping that produces closed blocks and the 1.2.7 T-junctions and right-angle turns.
Height-field construction: sum of radial bumps vs low-octave smoothed noise; resolution; whether water carving modifies it.
Density-field construction: the highway ridge term, and how Low/Medium/High map to amplitude versus spread. Also whether printed population is the field integral or derived from building count.
Water shape generation for coast, river and island is entirely undocumented, as is how 1.2.5 made rivers 'narrower and more meandering'.
Field tiling primitive: strip cuts, recursive OBB split, or polar sectoring around the centre? Plus the inset distance that creates the lanes and the numeric compactness/aspect thresholds.
Pier placement: what 'if a layout allows' means, and the location-quality predicate the creator never solved.
Tree candidate generation (Poisson-disc? jittered grid?), the 'Some trees' patch generator, and the clearance radii around houses, roads and trails.
Isoline extraction and the 'built more evenly across a map' resampling - stated as the fix for overlapping hachures but never described.

What exactly the permalink encodes, and which subsystems besides tree coverage have independently rerollable RNG streams.
Why two intersecting highways (crossroads) proved hard - whatever couples highway, density field and square is apparently single-highway-shaped.

techniques.name: Two-phase pipeline: population/buildings first, geometry second
techniques.algorithm_summary: Phase 1 builds people+buildings from a dependency graph until the population target; phase 2 lays a road network large enough to hold them, then places outer landscape. Inverts watabou's geometry-first order.
techniques.biggest_unknown: How the building count is translated into a target settlement area/stage quota.

techniques.name: Priority-queue road growth with green 'proposed roads'
techniques.algorithm_summary: Min-priority queue of road proposals {start, dir, type, priority}. Pop lowest; jitter dir by U(-maxAngle,+maxAngle); extend roadLength m; snap/extend/reject via local constraints; insert; after N segments push a perpendicular left+right proposal pair. nextPriority = curr + spokePriorityChange for main spokes, +1 for offshoots.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Exact local-constraint thresholds (min road separation, snap radius) and retry/discard policy.

techniques.name: PSLG with incremental lot (face) detection
techniques.algorithm_summary: Roads form a planar straight-line graph with enforced intersections; inserting an edge triggers lot detection that finds newly created faces and the face just split in two. Lots carry metadata (already used?). Payload shows 5326 edges / 4303 vertices with adjacency lists and 14 edge types.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Whether faces are maintained via half-edge DCEL or re-walked on demand.

techniques.name: Stage boundary prune-and-trim
techniques.algorithm_summary: Between stages, unconnected normal roads are pruned (dangling chains deleted) and main roads trimmed back to the settlement's current perimeter. Visible in the road-growth GIFs.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Exact definition of 'perimeter' (union of used lots vs alpha-shape).

techniques.name: Branch type: Continue vs Curve-around-origin
techniques.algorithm_summary: Continue = branch perpendicular then run straight with per-segment jitter (warped grid). Curve around origin = branched roads hold a fixed radius from the settlement centre, re-projecting each segment onto the circle tangent, producing concentric rings.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Whether radius is fixed at branch time or re-derived per segment.

techniques.name: District lot recursive binary split to target area
techniques.algorithm_summary: New roads split lots into two until every face is under a max area (Regenerate tool exposes 'Divide lots to area', default 10000 m2, with a selectable dividing road type). District stages use minDistrictArea (70k-100k m2) to merge undersized district lots into a neighbour.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Where the split line is placed (OBB long-axis bisection assumed) and how it connects to existing intersections.

techniques.name: Lot -> plots -> buildings, with Dense/Gaps/Individually-placed modes
techniques.algorithm_summary: Lot interior is partitioned into rectangular plots (edge-driven inward strips). Dense = plots tiled wall-to-wall; Gaps = same tiling then each footprint inset; Individually placed = template shapes (L, rectangle) fitted into plots. 'Anywhere in lot' flag switches between frontage-only and all-edges placement. Suburb density is P(plot gets a building).
techniques.biggest_unknown: Plot frontage/depth targets, corner resolution, and the template shape catalogue.

techniques.name: Suburb stage: perimeter ring + offshoots with invisible lot edges
techniques.algorithm_summary: Creates a perimeter road around the built core (createPerimeterSpokes, spacing = 5 x roadLength), then grows short offshoots (1-2 segments) from it and from main roads, making small lots immediately. Fringe buildings still live in lots, but some lot edges are rendered invisible. spokePriorityChange controls ribbon-vs-blob shape.
techniques.biggest_unknown: How the perimeter polyline is derived from the built lots and how roundedEdges fillets it.

techniques.name: Outer settlement: extend mains to border, subdivide to feature count
techniques.algorithm_summary: Main roads are extended to the map border, defining large outside lots; the generator estimates how many lots are needed for outer buildings + landscape features and binary-splits until that count is reached, then assigns features with an adjacency preference for like-with-like.
techniques.biggest_unknown: The estimation formula and the clustering/assignment heuristic.

techniques.name: Coast: two arms, overall spline shape then detail erosion
techniques.algorithm_summary: Two arms start near map centre and grow to the map edge. Overall shape (Smooth/Gentle/Sharp curves) sets large-scale bays/headlands; a second pass 'erodes' detail (Bays/Deep bays/Rough/Jagged); an 'ease into detail' envelope tapers amplitude near the settlement centre. Stretches are classified bay vs headland and decorated accordingly (bay texture weights, headland rocks, inset cliff/forest band).
techniques.biggest_unknown: Whether detail erosion is midpoint displacement, noise, or bay-template stamping; the bay/headland classifier.

techniques.name: Rivers: single path then convergent/divergent branches with island rule
techniques.algorithm_summary: One river path first (Straight/Gentle/Sharp), then branches from any existing stretch; convergent branches point upstream, divergent downstream. A branch that hits an existing river connects and stops, forming an island. Width in metres; minDistanceBetweenBridges gates road crossings.
techniques.biggest_unknown: The path generator itself and how bend-back-into-the-ocean failures are (not) handled.

techniques.name: Water as a road constraint: bridges over rivers, hard stop at oceans
techniques.algorithm_summary: Road legality checks reject proposals ending in water; rivers may be bridged subject to a minimum bridge spacing, oceans terminate roads. A protected circular exclusion zone at the settlement origin forbids any water body.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Radius of the exclusion disc and the bridge-selection rule.

techniques.name: Dependency graph with virtual-population scheduling
techniques.algorithm_summary: 80 resource nodes, each 1-per-N-people or 1-per-N-of-other-nodes, internally normalised to per-person ratios. The generator runs a pretend population counter that races ahead of the real one to minimise unemployment (alwaysPlaceWorkplace). Each node has lifestyle-banded core building pools plus a shop pool used when core buildings are impossible or by a probability (0.1 inside / 0.5 outside).
techniques.biggest_unknown: Tie-breaking when several nodes are simultaneously due.

techniques.name: Building pool tags drive district typing
techniques.algorithm_summary: 209 buildings carry 13 poolTags (CRAFTS_COMMERCIAL, LUXURY_COMMERCIAL, WATERFRONT, INDUSTRIAL, RED_LIGHT_DISTRICT...). District type for a new lot is chosen from 'remaining unplaced buildings and what the lot is next to' - i.e. matching outstanding tagged stock to the 17 district configs.
techniques.biggest_unknown: The actual scoring function and how residentialDistrictOrder=MOST_POPULOUS feeds in.

techniques.name: Straight-skeleton roofs computed at render time
techniques.algorithm_summary: 3D roof mode generates roofs per render (explicitly not stored server-side) that 'bend to follow the shape of a building'. The L-shaped sample shows a ridge following the L, 45-degree hip ends and a valley at the reflex corner - the signature of a straight skeleton.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Whether it is a true straight skeleton or a cheaper inward-offset approximation.

techniques.name: Lazy person materialisation with index-encoded appearance
techniques.algorithm_summary: Only a few key fields per person are persisted; the rest is generated on selection and locked in on manual edit. Appearance options are stored by index into the race's option table, so editing the race retroactively rewrites un-persisted people and reindexes edited ones.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Which fields are in the persisted minimal set.

techniques.name: Decoration areas filled at render time
techniques.algorithm_summary: Forests and rock/tree areas are stored as a shape plus density and randomly filled with lower-detail decorations when the map renders; individual decorations store explicit coordinates and carry more detail.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Whether the render-time fill is seeded (i.e. stable across reloads).

techniques.name: Harbour carving with wall-arm and pier templates
techniques.algorithm_summary: A template polygon (Rectangle / Semi-octagon / Semi-hexagon / L wide / L narrow) is subtracted from the waterfront district's land, a paved quay band follows the new edge, mole arms (single/two, follow-coast or stick-out) spring from the mouth corners leaving an entrance gap, and evenly spaced piers (straight or fishbone-branching, wood or stone) line the quay.
techniques.biggest_unknown: How the harbour's position and orientation on the coast are chosen and how arm length scales.

top_insights: FTG inverts the watabou order: it simulates population and buildings FIRST (dependency graph to a population target), then grows a road network big enough to hold them - so map size, district count and stage quotas are all downstream of a socio-economic model, not of geometry.

The road generator is a min-priority queue of 'proposed roads' (the green crosses in the guide's GIFs) over a planar graph with incremental face detection; the doc gives the priority rule literally: nextSegmentPriority = currPriority + mainSpokePriorityIncrease, offshoots always +1, lowest priority processed next - and that single number is the main ribbon-vs-blob shape control.

Lots are graph faces, not subdivided polygons. Everything downstream (district merging under minDistrictArea, recursive binary splitting to a max area, water fill, background fill, regeneration) reuses that one face structure, which is why the editor insists roads 'must have properly defined intersections'.

The full enum space is recoverable without touching the bundle: steps.jsonl captured document.body.innerText, giving verbatim complete option lists (6 layout presets, 11 materials, 4 wall types, 7 initial road patterns, 3 district counts, 3 placements, 2 branch types, 2 wall placements).

Units are settled: 1 internal unit = 1 metre (GeoJSON doc + form labels 'Road segment length (m)', 'Minimum district area (m2)'), and the persisted protobuf is integer centimetres - 500000 units across a CITY whose preset width is 5000 m.

Captured Medieval-europe CITY parameters in full: 2 district stages (DENSE 20% then GAPS 50%, roadLength 50/60 m, minDistrictArea 100000/70000 m2, branch segments 4/4 then 3/3, maxAngle 15 deg, new-main-road chance 0.5 then 0.1, wall after stage 1) plus a suburb stage taking the remaining 30% (roadLength 30 m, density 0.8, offshoot sections 1-2, branch probability 0.75, perimeter spokes every 5x roadLength).

Building placement modes are cheap variations on one tiling: Dense tiles the frontage band wall-to-wall; Gaps is the SAME tiling with every footprint inset ('and then shrunk'); only 'Individually placed' fits template shapes. The three material samples are pixel-identical geometry in three colours.

Coast generation is explicitly two-stage and two-armed: arms grow from map centre to map edge, an overall spline sets bays/headlands, then a detail pass 'erodes' the line with an amplitude envelope that tapers near the settlement so the harbour lands somewhere sane.

The dependency graph's scheduler uses a virtual population counter that runs ahead of the real one because FTG prioritises minimising unemployment - which means default output deliberately does NOT match the configured per-person ratios unless alwaysPlaceWorkplace is turned off.

People are stored lazily: only a few fields persist and the rest regenerate on access, with appearance options encoded as indices into the race's option tables - a storage decision with documented, user-visible retroactive-edit hazards.

Plot generation is never described: target frontage/depth, corner resolution, residual interior handling, and the 'Individually placed' template shape catalogue.
Which field(s) does the settlement-level 'Number of districts' (Less/Normal/More) scale? It is absent from layoutParameters.
The district-type selection function - how 'remaining unplaced buildings' and 'what the lot is next to' are scored, and how residentialDistrictOrder=MOST_POPULOUS participates.
Road legality constants: minimum separation between roads, parallelism test, and the generation-time snap radius (distinct from the editor's user-facing snapping distance).
Failure handling: are rejected road proposals retried or discarded, and can a stage restart? A CITY took ~300 s wall time to generate, which hints at an expensive loop or a retry budget.
Coast detail 'erosion': midpoint displacement, arclength-sampled noise, or bay-template stamping? And how is a stretch classified as bay vs headland?
How the two coast arms are seeded near the map centre and joined without a visible seam.
Wall geometry for AROUND_ALL_LOTS: polygon offset or lot-edge following, and where gates/towers are placed. Castle 'moat' and 'cliff' options exist in the JSON but are null and undocumented.
perimeterSpokeDistanceMultiplier=5 is multiplied by what exactly, and how is the perimeter polyline derived from the built lots?

Is generation deterministic from a seed? decoration areas are explicitly filled 'when the map is rendered' and 3D roofs are computed per render, so some randomness may not be reproducible from the saved file.
Building name/description generation and the building-type -> sub-location set -> job-posting mapping are named everywhere and specified nowhere.
District naming: the payload carries both a descriptive name ('Beer Forest', 'Ash Town') and a contracted form ('Ashton', 'Greenwood') - the morphology rule is unknown.

techniques.name: Integer-centimetre coordinate space on a fixed square canvas
techniques.algorithm_summary: All geometry is unsigned varint, 1 unit = 1 cm, extent 0..500000 = 5000 m square. Derived from presets.json sizes (CITY width=5000 m) + coordinates saturating at 500000, then confirmed 3x by roadLength params (50/60/30 m) reproducing as measured edge-length modes and by the on-screen scale bar. NOTE: create-request's blankSettlementWidth=3500 applies only to size BLANK and is NOT the map width.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Whether +y is screen-north or screen-south; needs a direct pixel-to-coordinate calibration.

techniques.name: Typed road graph with redundant adjacency lists
techniques.algorithm_summary: 5326 edges {id,a,b,type} + 4303 nodes {id,{x,y},packed adjacency}. Adjacency is exactly consistent with the edge list (sum/2 = 5326, 0 mismatches). 10 edge types with distinct length signatures. Degree histogram: 1.9% deg-1 (cul-de-sacs tolerated), 62.2% deg-2, 22.5% deg-3, 13.0% deg-4, max deg 6. Roads are emergent chains of 2-valent nodes, not first-class objects.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Semantic names for the 10 edge-type enum values (only length/ context signatures recovered).

techniques.name: Hard 15-degree per-vertex turn clamp on core streets
techniques.algorithm_summary: Deviation-from-straight at degree-2 nodes, binned at 1 degree, falls off a cliff at exactly 15 for edge types 0,1,2,10 (bins 10-14 populated, bin 15+ empty). Matches STATED maxMainRoadAngle=15 / maxNormalRoadAngle=15. Suburb (type 4) and rural (type 6) run to ~43-45 deg, so the cap is class-specific. Full deg-2 distribution is bimodal: 30.5% within 2.5 deg, second mass exactly at 90 deg (lattice corners).
techniques.biggest_unknown: Why suburb/rural classes exceed 15 deg despite the same declared parameter.

techniques.name: Spoke-and-lattice staged growth
techniques.algorithm_summary: Ordered stages each consume proportionOfBuildings (0.2 dense core, 0.5 second ring, 0.3 suburb). Roads grow by extending radial spokes that stochastically demote (spokeStaySpokeProbability 0.5 then 0.1), max 1 new spoke per stage, branchType CONTINUE; each branch grows a local rectangular lattice of verticalBranchSegments x horizontalBranchSegments (4x4 then 3x3) at roadLength 50/60/30 m. Junction arm angles median 90.02 deg (locally orthogonal) but the global heading spectrum is flat (max bin 8.0%) - each lattice carries its own arbitrary rotation.
techniques.biggest_unknown: The actual spoke seeding/extension rule and how lattices are stitched where two frames collide.

techniques.name: Blocks as road-graph faces with a ~1750 m2 target
techniques.algorithm_summary: Lot group type 18 holds 901 block polygons, median 1764 m2, 4-6 verts. Block edge lengths cluster at 30 m (43% of 5910 edges) and 60 m, exactly the stage roadLengths, so blocks are the faces of the road lattice. Mean 3.39 buildings per block (median 2, max 133); 12.9% empty. Occupied blocks: 2977 m2 / 3.89 buildings = 766 m2 per building against a 433 m2 footprint = ~57% coverage.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Whether an explicit sub-split toward a target area runs after face extraction (the 1700 m2 mode suggests yes).

techniques.name: Rectangle-first building placement with plot-driven shearing
techniques.algorithm_summary: 2798 closed rings; true vertex counts 4->2514 (90%), 5->188, 3->9. Rectangularity (area/min-area-rect) median 0.98, 50.4% >= 0.98. Quad worst-corner deviation from 90 deg: median 0.91 deg but p95=27.5, p99=68.5 - most are true rectangles, a minority sheared to fill awkward plots. OBB long 22.98 m / short 18.82 m median, aspect 1.21. Mean footprint 433.8 m2. Only 8.6% share a vertex with a neighbour: terraces are tight packing, not shared walls.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Why only ~48% are axis-locked to their street (31.8% within 5 deg + 16.4% at 85-90 deg) instead of ~100%.

techniques.name: Frontage detection and entrance stamping
techniques.algorithm_summary: Field 8.6 carries an entrance point lying exactly on the building outline (median 0.01 m off) and median 4.56 m from the nearest road. Angle between centroid->entrance direction and the road direction is median 77.9 deg with 38.9% in the 85-90 deg bin: the door is placed on the face pointing at the street. 82.2% of buildings have a polygon corner within 2 m of a road centreline. 109/2798 (3.9%) get no entrance at all.
techniques.biggest_unknown: What makes 3.9% of buildings fail to receive an entrance.

techniques.name: Typed land-use lot groups (blocks / plazas / 6 crop fields / forest / reserve)
techniques.algorithm_summary: Field 9 = 11 groups / 1176 lots, each lot {id, closed ring, type, flagA, flagB}. Group 18 = 901 building blocks (median 1764 m2, 66.6% of buildings inside). Group 8 = 15 plaza lots (unique flags 1,1). Six groups (0,1,3,11,12,13) of 30-40 lots at ~10 ha each = farm fields by crop, matching the six availableRawResources. Group 4 = 2 forest polygons (6.35 + 7.27 km2, byte-identical to the tree-layer regions). Group 20 = 4 reserved natural areas. flagB cleanly separates render classes: 0 in-town, 1 plaza, 2 outside-settlement.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Group type 2 mixes ~1700 m2 town parcels with multi-km2 background masks under one enum value.

techniques.name: District rings, label anchors and two-tier naming
techniques.algorithm_summary: Field 10 = {id, long name, short name (optional), label anchor {x,y}, boundary ring, prose summary}. The map draws the SHORT name, falling back to the long one (Rustic Village->Ticwick, Ash Town->Ashton, Green Wood->Greenwood; Beer Forest has no short form and shows the long one). Districts split off when a region exceeds minDistrictArea (10 ha then 7 ha). 71% of buildings fall inside some ring; 411 m2 of district land per building.
techniques.biggest_unknown: The district typing rule that produces the 17 archetypes and the prose summary's 'overall X, but also contains Y' composition.

techniques.name: Non-simple district rings (shipped failure mode)
techniques.algorithm_summary: Rasterised area vs shoelace area per district: 1.03, 4.47, 1.01, 1.00. Rustic Village's ring self-intersects, so a non-zero-winding fill inverts part of it. Every ring also contains duplicate consecutive vertices (min segment length 0.0 m). A consumer must use even-odd/raster fill or repair the ring.
techniques.biggest_unknown: Whether self-intersection is generic or specific to districts that wrap a coastline; one sample only.

techniques.name: Water outlines resampled to a uniform 100 m arc step
techniques.algorithm_summary: Four polygons: the sea (5.59 km2 of 25, touching 5 map-edge points), two river reaches, one small basin. Median segment length is 99.9-100.0 m on ALL four, so water is generated as a coarse path then walked at fixed arc length. The render shows smooth curves, so the client must smooth/spline at draw time.
techniques.biggest_unknown: The river generator itself (maxConvergences/maxDivergences/generationShape were all null/preset).

techniques.name: Wall serialised as a tower chain only
techniques.algorithm_summary: Field 7 = 17 objects {id,{x,y},scale 1.0,kind 7} that in id order form an open polyline with 37.9-101.3 m segments and smoothly varying headings. All 17 are also vertices of the Beer Forest district ring (11 shared with Rustic Village, 6 with Ash Town), matching STATED wallPlacement=AROUND_ALL_LOTS after stage 1. The render shows a slate crenellated band with round tower discs at those intervals; the band geometry is NOT in the payload, so the client strokes the tower polyline.
techniques.biggest_unknown: How the band is generated from the chain (offset polygon vs stroked polyline with crenellation tiling) and where gates are.

techniques.name: Sprite decoration layers with round-robin variant assignment
techniques.algorithm_summary: Each layer carries 7 opaque 4-char asset keys plus instances {variant 0..6, {x,y}, f32 scale}. 4125 trees split 590/590/589/589/589/589/589 - dead even, i.e. round-robin, not random. All 4125 scales are exactly 1.0, so the visible size variation lives in the sprite art. Two sibling layers (coniferous, palm) have 7 assets and ZERO instances, matching the STATED climate proportions 100/0/0 - this identifies the layers.

techniques.name: Tree scatter is density-target random, NOT Poisson-disc
techniques.algorithm_summary: 4125 tree nearest-neighbour distances: mean 15.94 m, median 14.14 m, p5 3.60, p95 33.45, MIN 0.28 m. The absence of any hard minimum rules out Poisson-disc/blue-noise; the broad unimodal hump peaking at 10-12 m is consistent with independent uniform sampling inside region polygons at a density target, with deliberate overlap for canopy clumps. Upper-class residential: 0.5 {GRASS,TREES,FENCES}, 0.3 {GRASS,TREES}, 0.1 each of {BANDSTAND}{STATUE}{MONUMENT}{FOUNTAIN} and those +{TREES}. techniques.algorithm_summary: MIT module by FTG's author overlays a full-window iframe of the live site on a fixed 5000x5000 Foundry scene (= the CITY map width in metres, 1 unit = 1 m). postMessage JSON {type,data}, origin-checked. FTG->module: BUILDING, DISTRICT, FACTIONS, BUILDINGS, PEOPLE, NEW_PLAYER_CURRENT_LOCATION, NEW_SETTLEMENT_TIME, BUILDING_UPDATE, PERSON_UPDATE, PEOPLE_UPDATE, BUILDINGS_UPDATE, PIN/PIN_UPDATED/PIN_DELETED, OPEN_EXTERNAL_CALENDAR, MOUSE_MOVE (re-dispatched so Foundry drag survives the overlay). module->FTG adds SIMULATE_TIME, CREATE_EVENT, FAVOURITE_*, *_NOTE. techniques.name: Visual language: flat fills, diagonal roof split, single upper-left light
techniques.algorithm_summary: Sampled palette: sea #67819c, nearshore #7795b3, harbour #7a99b8, pasture #a4c28e, ploughed #a08d7f, wheat #efdfa7, forest #849c6b, town lawn #adb69d, paving #c6c2bb (edge #bbb7b1), wood #81695b/#846a5a (shaded #745d4f), stone #686a6e/#787a7e, wall #6f7276 with #535659 edging, pier #bcb8b2. Buildings are flat polygons with a diagonal tonal split (cheap pitched-roof read) plus a soft lower-right drop shadow; trees carry the same shadow direction, so one global light. Roads are filled mitred bands, not strokes. Fields are separated by hedgerow lines of tree sprites on a perfectly straight 100 m lattice. Coast: sea -> nearshore lightening -> white foam line -> tan beach -> grass. District labels are serif Title Case, black with a cream halo, set on a curve (the older 2023-era render used horizontal white small-caps instead).
